posts.title: A good teacher teaches more than just the subject
posts.summary: Some can explain the universe but cannot practice basic human decency.
posts.html:
A great teacher does not merely transfer knowledge from one mind to another. They create the psychological environment in which a student actually wants to learn.

There is something profoundly beautiful about a good teacher. Not merely someone who possesses an extraordinary command of their subject, or someone capable of explaining the most complex of concepts with remarkable simplicity, but someone whose very presence transforms the atmosphere of a classroom.

We’ve all encountered teachers who make us genuinely look forward to attending their lectures. Teachers whose enthusiasm is contagious, whose personalities shine through their explanations, and whose warmth makes even the most intimidating subjects seem approachable. Their classrooms become places of curiosity rather than obligation, where students feel comfortable asking questions, challenging ideas, laughing at mistakes, and discovering the joy of learning.

What makes such teachers remarkable is not necessarily the depth of their knowledge, but their ability to make students want to acquire that knowledge.

And then, unfortunately, there exists another kind of teacher.

The pathetic, piece of shit , despicable authoritarian who confuses fear with respect. The human failure who mistakes humiliation for discipline, obedience for intelligence, and intimidation for authority. The teacher who treats a student’s innocent question as an inconvenience, their confusion as stupidity, and their mistakes as opportunities for public embarrassment.

Such individuals may possess impressive academic credentials. They may have spent decades mastering their disciplines. They may even be technically competent at explaining difficult concepts.

But what good is intellectual brilliance in a classroom where students are afraid to speak, where students have to be afraid of incurring punishments just for being 1 minute late to the lecture ?

A student who fears being ridiculed for asking a question will eventually stop asking questions. A student repeatedly humiliated for making mistakes may begin to associate learning itself with embarrassment. And a classroom governed by intimidation may produce outward obedience while quietly extinguishing the very curiosity that education is supposed to cultivate.

There is an important distinction between being a demanding teacher and being a cruel one. A great teacher can maintain exceptionally high standards while treating students with dignity. Intellectual rigor and human kindness are not opposing virtues.

Indeed, some of the most inspiring teachers are precisely those who push their students hardest, while making it abundantly clear that failure is an opportunity to improve rather than a reason for humiliation.

Students may forget much of what they were taught, but they often remember how their teachers made them feel about learning, about their abilities, and ultimately, about themselves.

And perhaps that is why the legacy of a truly great teacher extends far beyond the walls of a classroom.

posts.title: Self-hosted Smart Home Automation and AI infrastructure
posts.summary: How a Sony Vaio in Pune Led to Buffy Lab, My Self-Hosted AI and Smart Home Lab
posts.html:
My first homelab ran on an old, used Sony Vaio laptop. After that, I bought my own refurbished HP Elitedesk 800 G1 to play around with Proxmox in 2023. Three years later, the machine I call Buffy runs machine learning experiments, hosts my development tools, and helps decide how much heat my house in Buffalo needs.

Those sound like three different projects. They grew out of the same habit. When I use a system, I eventually want to understand what happens beneath the interface. What is doing the work? Where does the data go? What breaks when one of the components disappears? Self-hosting gives me a way to find out. If I want to know why a service is slow, why an experiment failed, or why my bedroom feels like a sauna in winter, I can follow the problem all the way down.

This is the story of how I became a lifelong homelabber, and why now I can’t live my life as an AI engineer without it.

The progression from my first Proxmox experiments to Buffy Lab. Diagram of the documented milestones.

2023–2024 · My first personal cloud in Pune

I started around August 2023 by installing Proxmox on an old Sony Vaio. I spent about a month experimenting with it. On my ASUS laptop, I also ran CasaOS inside a small virtual machine to get a feel for installing and managing applications packaged as Docker images. By December 2023, I had bought my first dedicated server, an HP EliteDesk 800 G1 with a fourth-generation Core i5-4690S, 16 GB of RAM, and a 1 TB SSD. I installed Proxmox 8.0 on it.

The machine gave me a reason to learn things I could previously explain only in theory. Installing a bare-metal hypervisor meant I had to think about the host, the guest OS, and where data actually lived. Getting applications to start meant learning Docker and using Portainer to manage containers. Reaching an application from another network sent me down a rabbit hole involving DNS, reverse proxies, ports, and TLS. Troubleshooting the whole thing meant getting comfortable with Linux from the command line.

I registered a domain through Hostinger and configured DNS and CNAME records. I set up Nginx as a reverse proxy, worked through port forwarding and SSL/TLS certificate configuration, and set up Cloudflare Tunnel with cloudflared to reach selected services remotely. I also set up Tailscale for private access to other services while away from home. It was my first practical introduction to the idea that an app’s URL, the route to the machine, and the policy for who can access it are separate decisions.

My early self-hosting experiments covered almost every category I could find:

  • Media and personal cloud. I ran Jellyfin as a media server and experimented with qBittorrent and the Arr ecosystem to automate parts of my media workflow. I hosted Nextcloud for personal files and explored TrueNAS. I learned to mount external drives, worked with Linux filesystems, and tried NFS, SFTP, and FileZilla.

  • Web hosting and databases. I hosted a WordPress site and a self-hosted search engine. I also explored a LAMP setup and worked with MariaDB and phpMyAdmin. I wanted to see what a web host was doing on my behalf, from the web server through the database.

  • Network-wide services. I tried AdGuard and Pi-hole for DNS filtering across my devices, including my Android TV. It made DNS tangible. A choice on the server could change how multiple devices on the network resolved requests.

  • Remote development and operations. I hosted browser-based VS Code, Apache Guacamole for remote desktops, Gitea for Git hosting, and Netdata for monitoring. I explored Kasm Workspaces and Arch Linux, and used the networking problems I ran into as a practical way to study CCNA fundamentals.

  • Early local AI. I tried hosting small language models for private use. The attempt never turned into a setup I could rely on. I kept coming back to the idea because I wanted to know what it would take to run useful AI workloads on hardware I controlled.

I wrote up that first phase in September 2024. At the time, I thought of the machine mainly as a personal cloud and an excuse to learn systems administration. The list of applications mattered because each one gave me a different reason to learn what the server was doing. My original homelab journal

2026 · I built Buffy around the work I wanted to do

By the time I was working on AI projects in Buffalo, my needs had changed. I wanted a machine that could run a GPU job, keep the resulting artifacts somewhere I could find them, and let me check what happened from my laptop. I also wanted a development environment I could reach remotely and a home automation setup I could extend with my own hardware.

Buffy is an HP Z440 Xeon workstation running Ubuntu 24.04 LTS on bare metal, with an NVIDIA RTX 4060 Ti and 16 GB of VRAM. Proxmox was where I learned virtualization. On this workstation, I chose to work directly on Ubuntu and use Docker Compose to define the supporting services. That gives me a direct path to the NVIDIA GPU from the host and a repeatable way to manage the applications around it. Compose also gives me somewhere to look when I need to reconstruct how a service was configured, how it connects to its dependencies, or where it keeps persistent data.

How the main systems on Buffy fit together. Conceptual architecture.

I organize the machine around the work I do on it. Dashy is my private launcher and Portainer is where I manage containers and stacks. I use code-server, JupyterLab, and Buffy Workbench for development, notebooks, and research runs, logs, and artifacts. I’ve used Sunshine for remote desktop streaming and IT-Tools for everyday developer utilities. PostgreSQL and MariaDB support relational workloads, and Valkey covers in-memory use cases. I’ve used pgAdmin, phpMyAdmin, Adminer, and DBGate in the database tooling. Paperless-ngx gives documents a searchable home, with Paperless-GPT for AI-assisted document workflows and Apache Tika and Gotenberg handling extraction and conversion. I use n8n for workflows and ntfy for notifications.

My Buffy service dashboard, as shown on the public project site.

One distinction I care about is who gets access to what. I use Cloudflare Tunnel for selected routes, including remote SSH in my setup, and Tailscale to reach private services from my devices. Dashy gave me a reminder that connectivity is specific to each service. Other applications were reachable over Tailscale while the dashboard was inaccessible from outside my home network. That narrowed the troubleshooting to the service’s own path, including how it listened and how it was published through Tailscale Serve. It’s a small example of how running the stack forces me to separate a healthy network from a healthy application route. Buffy Lab service inventory

The MLOps stack · Making a GPU run worth coming back to

A GPU lets me run a model. The infrastructure around it determines what I can learn from the run. If I come back two weeks later and can’t identify the dataset revision, reconstruct the settings, or locate the checkpoint, I have to repeat work before I can answer a research question. I wanted to make the context of an experiment as easy to find as its output.

I built a reusable workflow around Python, PyTorch, and JupyterLab on the RTX workstation. Git tracks the code and configuration, and DVC gives large datasets and experiment inputs versions I can associate with that code. MinIO provides S3-compatible object storage for versioned data and generated outputs such as checkpoints, figures, and evaluation files. Prefect gives multi-step jobs a task structure so I can see where a flow failed. I built a Python SDK to give experiment code a consistent way to record context, measurements, and outputs.

The research workflow I designed around versioned inputs, GPU execution, artifacts and telemetry. Conceptual diagram.

The workflow starts with a dataset revision and a run configuration. I want the experiment record to tell me which model and code revision I used, which parameters and environment it ran with, where the artifacts ended up, and what the machine was doing when the job ran. Then I can change one variable and compare the outcome. In the more instrumented version of the platform, I built experiment lineage and failure capture, worked with PyTorch activation probes, gradient norm tracking, and TorchDynamo graph capture, and added an MCP interface for querying run and failure history in natural language. Those tools help when a curve tells me something went wrong and I need to figure out which part of the system deserves a closer look.

Cadence, my research-paper discovery app, is a concrete example of what I use the hardware for. I built its daily ingestion pipeline to pull more than 500 new arXiv and bioRxiv papers and embed them on the local RTX 4060 Ti. The application can reload its live search index as new papers become available. That gives the workstation a regular workload alongside notebooks, local inference, and computer vision experiments. I also see the same infrastructure being useful for my robotics and 3D reconstruction work, where a result can depend on exactly which images, frames, and settings went into it.

The next piece I want to publish is a single experiment someone else can follow from input to output, with a DVC revision, the task graph, an artifact manifest, and measured GPU behavior. My public docs describe the platform and how its components fit together. A published run would show how I actually use them together. GPU research platform · MLOps workflow

What I look at when something breaks

A GPU workstation running databases, development tools, and automation can fail in several different ways. A slow dashboard might point to a busy host, an application consuming resources, a container restarting, or a routing issue. I want different kinds of evidence available before I start changing things.

Prometheus collects time-series metrics. Node Exporter covers the Linux host and cAdvisor adds container-level resource data. Grafana is where I compare those signals over time. Alloy and Loki give me a path from log collection to searching logs across services. For quick checks, I use Beszel to inspect resource usage and Dozzle to look at live container logs. Uptime Kuma checks whether applications respond, and ntfy gives me a way to receive notifications away from the dashboard.

The monitoring tools I use to inspect host pressure, application behavior and service availability. Conceptual diagram.

When something becomes slow, I can start by checking CPU, memory, or disk pressure, narrow down the container involved, then line up its logs with a restart or deployment. A service check can tell me that an endpoint stopped responding. Metrics and logs give me a way to investigate what happened around the same time. That’s especially useful when I have several workloads competing for a single workstation. Observability case study

One of the biggest changes in how I use my homelab is that Buffy runs around the clock. I can leave an ML job running overnight, go to class, work from another device, and return to the results later. My RTX 4060 Ti has become a compute resource I can access throughout the day, with the surrounding infrastructure helping me manage the work.

The datasets, Python environment, GPU computation, and outputs live on Buffy. This lets me use a lightweight device to work with a machine that stays powered on and available at home.

I use Cloudflare Tunnel and Tailscale to reach the environment remotely. Cloudflare Tunnel provides routes to selected services, while Tailscale connects my devices privately. Through those connections, I can access my development tools, inspect a running experiment, read logs, or retrieve results while away from the workstation. I documented the Cloudflare foundations and a tour of this environment in my video. Watch my AI platform setup tour

Running workloads for hours at a time also changes what I need from the software around them. I use code-server and JupyterLab to develop and inspect experiments, with Buffy Workbench organizing projects, scripts, run logs, and artifacts. Docker Compose defines the supporting services, and Prefect provides orchestration for workflows with multiple steps. That gives me a structure for work such as preparing inputs, executing a computation, and collecting its outputs.

Cadence, my research-paper discovery application, gives this infrastructure a recurring workload. Its daily ingestion pipeline collects more than 500 papers from arXiv and bioRxiv, generates embeddings on the local RTX 4060 Ti, and updates the application’s search index. The same workstation supports my other Python, PyTorch, and computer vision experiments. Having persistent compute at home makes it easier to fit longer jobs around my schedule.

The GPU’s 16 GB of VRAM also makes resource requirements a practical part of experimentation. Model size, batch size, input resolution, and precision all affect whether a workload fits. When a run fails, I want enough information to understand which constraint I reached. My experiment instrumentation records context and failures, while Prometheus, Grafana, and Loki help me inspect resource behavior and logs. I can investigate a job alongside the other services sharing the workstation.

Keeping track of the outputs matters just as much as keeping the computation running. I use Git and DVC to associate experiments with code and dataset versions, and MinIO to store datasets and generated artifacts. When I return to a completed job, I want to locate its configuration, logs, checkpoints, and evaluation outputs together. That makes an overnight experiment something I can review and build on the next day.

This has made Buffy part of my everyday research workflow. I can prepare an experiment when I have time to think through it, let the machine execute the work over a longer period, and inspect the outcome remotely. The value of having a workstation available 24/7 is that my experiments can continue beyond the hours I spend sitting in front of them.

The Thermostat Wars · Teaching my house to pay attention to three rooms

The project that made Buffy feel like part of my home started because my bedroom kept overheating. The living-room thermostat was making decisions from one point in the house. My room had a vent that pushed a lot of hot air, while another bedroom could still feel cold. I could open my window in the middle of a Buffalo winter and end up with one side of the room freezing while the other was still too hot. Eventually, I decided I wanted to know what the temperatures were doing across the house and use those measurements to inform the thermostat.

I installed a Honeywell T6 Pro Z-Wave thermostat on the existing two-wire heating circuit and paired it with a Zooz 800-series Z-Wave USB controller connected to Buffy. Z-Wave JS UI bridges that connection into my self-hosted Home Assistant. The thermostat measures the living room and accepts setpoint requests through Home Assistant.

For the two bedrooms I built my own sensing nodes, each with an ESP8266 D1 Mini and a BME280. The BME280 measures temperature, humidity, and pressure over I²C. I ran ESPHome on Buffy to configure and flash the boards. The first assemblies booted and connected to Wi-Fi, but the I²C scanner kept reporting that it had found no devices. I got the same result on three attempts. Eventually I went back to the physical connections, removed the unreliable headers, and soldered the wires directly. The scanner finally found the BME280 at 0x76, followed by a live temperature reading of 24.1°C. I moved the nodes into the bedrooms, powered them from USB wall adapters, and brought their readings into Home Assistant through ESPHome over Wi-Fi.

The three-room sensing and thermostat integration, including its weighted inputs and bounded setpoint requests. Conceptual diagram.

Once all three readings were available, I created a Home Assistant template sensor that uses 20% of the living-room temperature and 40% from each bedroom. The units have to agree before the calculation because my firmware logs used Celsius and the Home Assistant climate interface used Fahrenheit. I set an initial target of 69°F with a band from 68.5°F to 69.5°F. Below the band, the automation can request more heat if the room conditions allow it. Above the band, it lowers the requested setpoint. Inside the band, it generally leaves the setpoint alone. If my bedroom reaches 72°F, that condition takes priority over a low weighted average. The initial requests are bounded between 68°F and 72°F, and a missing or invalid reading can trigger a 68°F fallback while Home Assistant is running.

The Honeywell still runs the furnace according to its own sensor and control logic. My automation adjusts the setpoint about every ten minutes when conditions call for a change. If the living room is colder than the lowered setpoint, the thermostat can still call for heat. If Buffy goes offline, the thermostat can continue operating independently, potentially at the last setpoint it received. Keeping that separation mattered to me because the workstation might be rebooting or running an experiment at the same time the house needs heat.

I built a Home Assistant dashboard for the three readings, the weighted value, and the thermostat state. The moment I knew the integration worked was when I watched an automation trace issue a setpoint request and then saw the Honeywell report the new setpoint back. That gave me an end-to-end test of a system spanning solder joints, Wi-Fi, a Z-Wave controller, a Docker-hosted application, and a physical thermostat. Full thermostat build story · Technical case study

The next layer · Expanding the lab without rebuilding it

By October I had also put together a separate Compose configuration for the next set of services. I organized it into profiles so I could try one group without restarting the applications I already depended on. The configuration covers Kopia for backups, changedetection.io for tracking web pages, Actual Budget for personal finance, and Miniflux for feeds. The productivity profile adds Syncthing, Karakeep, and Mealie. The development profile adds Forgejo and Open WebUI, with Open WebUI intended to use the existing Ollama runtime. I scoped Immich as a separate deployment for photo management.

That exercise got me thinking more carefully about recovery. A synced folder can propagate a deletion. A backup repository on the same disk leaves both copies exposed to a disk failure. My next step is to run a restore I can document, alongside the failover drill I’ve been planning for the home server and Hetzner. For those projects, the evidence I want is a record of what I recovered, how long it took, and what broke along the way.

What I made public

I put the architecture, service inventory, and case studies on the Buffy Lab site. The thermostat demo runs entirely in the browser. You can move the three room-temperature sliders and see how the weighted temperature, deadband, and bedroom rule interact. My actual Home Assistant instance and private administration tools stay separate from the site. I’m also preparing a controlled RTX inference playground. That’s a separate deployment from the public thermostat simulator, which you can already try.

I still enjoy the part of homelabbing I enjoyed on that Sony Vaio. I can take a problem that I only half understand, build something around it, and keep following the failures until I know more than I did when I started. In Pune that meant figuring out why a service couldn’t be reached from outside my network. In Buffalo it sometimes means figuring out why a model run went sideways, and sometimes it means finally finding a bad solder joint. I like having a place where I can work through both. Explore Buffy Lab and try the thermostat demo

posts.title: The Thermostat Wars: Revenge of the Engineer
posts.summary: How I stopped fighting my roommates over the heat and engineered a room-aware, locally automated HVAC controller.
posts.html:
There comes a point in every engineer’s life when a seemingly trivial inconvenience becomes so persistently annoying that the only reasonable response is to overengineer the living hell out of it.

For me, that inconvenience was my home’s thermostat.

Houses in Buffalo, New York, can’t survive the cold weather without heating. Now, you would assume that heating a 5 bedroom , 1 Hall and 1 kitchen house is a fairly straightforward problem. You set a temperature, your furnace turns on, warm air flows through the vents, and eventually everyone is comfortable. Simple enough, right?

Well, not quite.

You see, our house has a rather peculiar heating problem. The heat vents are disproportionately large, and the distribution of warm air between rooms is anything but uniform. While one room struggles to stay warm, another practically turns into a sauna. Unfortunately for me, my bedroom happens to fall into the latter category.

Making matters worse, I share this house with roommates who have their own very different ideas of what constitutes a comfortable temperature. When someone feels cold, they simply crank up the thermostat. The furnace obediently starts blasting heat through the house, and before long, I’m sitting in my room wondering whether I’ve accidentally relocated to the surface of the Sun. To make things worse, I keep the window fully open at night, in peak winters, to counter the heat waves of Sahara coming out of my room’s vents, which causes one side of my room to become Antartica and another to become insanely, suffocatingly hot.

There was even a rumor that the guy who used to live in my room before me used to suffer from nosebleeds in winters due to excess heating and hot, dry air from my bedroom’s air vents. Yes, it’s that serious.

Naturally, my first instinct was to look for simple solutions. Could I close the vents in my room? Not easily. Their physical construction makes that impractical, and restricting airflow without understanding the HVAC system could create pressure and airflow problems elsewhere. Could I ask our landlord for some solution? Nope. Could we simply agree on a reasonable thermostat setting?

Well, if you’ve ever lived with roommates, you probably know how that conversation goes.

After enough nights of unnecessary overheating, I realized something.

This wasn’t just a temperature problem. It was a control systems problem.

The dumb thermostat had no understanding of what was actually happening in individual rooms. It was making decisions based on a single temperature measurement, even though the house itself had wildly different temperature conditions depending on where you stood.

And instead of continually negotiating with people over a dial on the wall, why not give the heating system the information it was missing?

What if I could measure temperatures independently across multiple rooms, average or intelligently combine those readings, and use that information to control when the furnace runs? What if I could implement custom temperature thresholds, hysteresis, and minimum heating intervals to prevent unnecessary cycling? And what if the entire system could operate locally, without depending on a cloud service or an internet connection?

Better yet, what if the thermostat retained a safe, independent heating mode even when my home automation server was unavailable?

That sounded like a much more interesting problem to solve. The engineer in me was now fully awake.

So, I decided to take matters into my own hands.

Out went the old thermostat. In came a new programmable Z-Wave thermostat, a handful of inexpensive ESP microcontrollers, distributed temperature sensors, and a self-hosted Home Assistant instance running on my Ubuntu workstation.

At this point, I didn’t care what my landlord would say, given that I was modifying a home without permission, a rental which I am simply renting for some next few months: my mind was far too curious to explore the various smart home automations.

Of course, getting from a simple idea to a reliable system meant learning about thermostat wiring, low-voltage HVAC control, sensor communication, local networking, temperature regulation, and the subtle difference between making something smart and making something dependable.

This article is the story of how an everyday roommate disagreement, and suffocating heat from air vents, pushed me into building my own home heating control system, what I learned along the way, and why sometimes the best engineering projects begin with a very simple thought:

“Fine. I’ll build a better one myself.”

The New Thermostat

Luckily for me, our house has a fairly straightforward, conventional heating system rather than a more complicated multi-stage heating or heat-pump configuration.

Upon removing the old thermostat, I discovered just two wires: a red one (R) and a white one (W). The red wire supplies 24V AC from the heating system’s transformer, while the white wire carries the call-for-heat signal back to the furnace.

And that was it. No complicated wiring harness, no additional cooling or fan control connections, and most importantly, no C-wire (common wire) to worry about.

This was particularly convenient because the Honeywell T6 Pro Z-Wave thermostat I’d chosen supports battery-powered operation, meaning I could use the existing two-wire arrangement without having to run additional wiring through the walls.

Sometimes, engineering gets a little easier when the infrastructure you’re working with is decades old!

Luckily for me, the 2 wires were easy to install inside the new thermostat’s wall bracket clamp area, as I didn’t have to worry about soldering the wires to any terminals! I just inserted the 2 wires inside the W and the R terminals, and it fastened itself.

Smart Home Automation

Next, it was time for some adaptive heating automation, and a system I can easily control with the touch of a button on my mobile phone.

Now came the interesting part.

Replacing an old thermostat with a new programmable one is hardly a groundbreaking feat of engineering. Sure, I could now adjust the temperature without having to physically walk up to the thermostat, but that alone wasn’t going to solve my original problem.

The thermostat still measured only the temperature in the living room. The actual temperature of the air in its 5 feet radius vicinity. My bedroom would still turn into a furnace, my friends’ bedroom would still remain comparatively cold, and my roommates would still be engaged in their eternal struggle over the thermostat.

In other words, I had merely replaced a dumb thermostat with a more sophisticated thermostat that was, for my particular problem, still relatively dumb.

What I really wanted was something more ambitious.

I wanted the house to have an in-depth understanding of its own thermal conditions. I wanted temperatures from multiple rooms to influence the heating decisions. I wanted those decisions to be made automatically, according to rules I could design, inspect, and modify myself.

And since I already had an Ubuntu workstation running a miniature ecosystem of self-hosted services, why not make that computer the brain of the operation?

Building the Brain: Self-Hosting Home Assistant

My Ubuntu workstation, affectionately named Buffy, is an HP Z440 that I use for programming, machine-learning experiments, and various self-hosted homelab services.

Rather than purchase some proprietary smart-home hub that would require another account, another mobile application, and potentially a cloud subscription, I decided to deploy Home Assistant directly on Buffy.

Home Assistant is an open-source home-automation platform that can integrate devices from numerous manufacturers and coordinate them through a common interface.

More importantly for my purposes, it can run locally.

This was a significant design consideration.

I didn’t want my heating automation to depend on whether some company’s servers were functioning, whether its mobile app was online, or whether an internet connection happened to be available.

My ideal system would operate entirely within my local network, with the internet being a convenience rather than a requirement.

Since much of my existing homelab infrastructure was already containerized, I deployed Home Assistant using Docker.

For anyone unfamiliar with Docker, a container is essentially an isolated runtime environment that allows an application to run with its own dependencies without requiring you to install and configure everything directly on the host operating system.

This made it easier to manage Home Assistant alongside my other services and preserve its configuration between container restarts.

Once running, Home Assistant exposed a web interface on port 8123 of Buffy.

From my laptop or phone, I could access the application over my local network and inspect connected devices, sensor readings, automations, and system events.

At this point, I had the beginnings of a smart-home control center.

There was just one minor problem.

Home Assistant couldn’t magically communicate with my new thermostat.

The thermostat used Z-Wave, while my workstation knew absolutely nothing about Z-Wave.

That meant another piece of hardware.

Making the Honeywell Talk: Z-Wave and the Zooz USB Stick

My Honeywell T6 Pro uses Z-Wave, a wireless communication protocol designed primarily for smart-home devices.

Unlike conventional Wi-Fi devices, Z-Wave devices communicate through a separate, low-power wireless network. A Z-Wave thermostat doesn’t simply connect to your Wi-Fi router like a phone or laptop. It needs to communicate with a compatible Z-Wave controller. So, to bridge that gap, I purchased a Zooz 800 Series Z-Wave USB stick.

The stick looks like an ordinary USB dongle, but it contains the radio hardware required to create and manage a Z-Wave network. Then I connected it to Buffy, where Ubuntu detected it as a serial USB device. This introduced another small engineering detail: a USB device can appear under a name such as /dev/ttyACM0, but those device numbers aren’t necessarily permanent. Linux may assign a different identifier when devices are disconnected and reconnected. For a service that needs to run reliably, I preferred using the device’s persistent identifier under /dev/serial/by-id/. That path allowed me to identify the Zooz controller consistently and expose it to the appropriate Docker container.

But merely plugging the controller into a USB port was not enough. I still needed software capable of operating the Z-Wave network.

Enter Z-Wave JS UI

I deployed another self-hosted service: Z-Wave JS UI.

This application manages the Z-Wave controller and provides a way to discover, pair, configure, and inspect devices on the Z-Wave network.

My arrangement involved three distinct components:

  • Zooz USB stick: The physical radio that communicates with Z-Wave devices.

  • Z-Wave JS UI: The software that manages the radio and the Z-Wave network.

  • Home Assistant: The higher-level platform that uses the devices and incorporates them into automations.

Z-Wave JS UI provided a management interface on port 8091, while its WebSocket server allowed Home Assistant to communicate with the Z-Wave network.

In my setup, I connected Home Assistant to that server over port 3000.

I then put the Honeywell thermostat into Z-Wave inclusion mode and initiated the pairing process through Z-Wave JS UI.

After the device was included and its interview completed, Home Assistant finally recognized my thermostat.

And suddenly, I could see a whole set of useful information:

The current temperature in the living room. The desired heating setpoint. The thermostat’s operating mode. Its reported humidity. Whether the thermostat was actively requesting heating or simply sitting idle.

I could also send commands to it.

For example, Home Assistant could request that the Honeywell change its heating setpoint to 70°F without anyone touching the thermostat.

That was a rather satisfying moment. I must admit I was very thrilled!

I had successfully connected a conventional residential heating system to a locally hosted automation platform using a dedicated wireless protocol and a Linux computer.

And because the thermostat itself retained its own temperature sensor and control logic, I hadn’t needed to replace the actual furnace controller with some homemade electronic contraption.

But this was still only half the story.

The thermostat could now listen to Buffy. The next challenge was teaching Buffy to listen to the rest of the house.

An Idea I Came Up With: Why Not Average the Temperatures?

This was the conceptual turning point of the project.

While thinking about how to solve the uneven heating, I came up with my own original idea that seemed surprisingly straightforward.

What if the thermostat didn’t have to depend exclusively on the temperature of the room in which it was installed?

What if I placed temperature sensors inside the bedrooms, collected their readings, and calculated a representative temperature for the entire house?

Instead of deciding whether to heat based only on the living room, I could make the decision using information from all the rooms that actually mattered.

Initially, I thought of taking a simple average.

Suppose the temperatures were:

Room temperature of :

Living room: 69°F

My bedroom: 71°F

Friend’s bedroom: 65°F

The average would be:

(69 + 71 + 65) / 3 = 68.3°F

That already seemed more useful than looking at the living room’s 69°F alone.

But then I realized something else.

Why should all three rooms have equal importance?

The living room was not where the overheating problem originated. The real conflict was between my bedroom, which heated quickly, and one of my roommate’s bedroom, which tended to remain cold.

A simple arithmetic mean would treat every room identically, even though our comfort requirements and heating problems were different.

That led me to a second idea. Instead of using an ordinary average, why not assign different weights to each room?

I decided to start with the following weights:

Room Weight :

Living room: 20% ( where no one sleeps, or stays for long anyways)

My bedroom: 40%

Friend’s bedroom: 40%

This produces:

T(weighted) = 0.2 × T(living) + 0.4 × T(mine) + 0.4 × T(friend)

For the temperatures in the example above:

T(weighted) = 0.2(69) + 0.4(71) + 0.4(65) = 68.2°F

The bedrooms now collectively determine 80% of the calculated temperature.

And that was another advantage of implementing the system through software.

I could change the weights whenever I wanted.

Perhaps my bedroom should be given more importance at night. Perhaps the colder bedroom should be prioritized during the day. Perhaps I could eventually calculate weights dynamically based on occupancy or observed heating behavior.

The point was that the system would no longer be limited to one fixed measurement.

It would have multiple observations and a decision-making strategy that I could design myself.

There was still one glaring practical obstacle.

I needed actual temperature sensors in those rooms.

And that meant getting my hands dirty with electronics.

Building My Own Wireless Temperature Sensors

I considered buying ready-made wireless temperature sensors.

They would certainly have been easier. I could have purchased them, paired them with Home Assistant, and probably completed the project much sooner.

But where’s the fun in that?

I wanted to build at least part of the system myself.

After exploring inexpensive embedded hardware, I settled on two components:

ESP8266 D1 Mini microcontrollers and BME280 environmental sensors.

The ESP8266 is a small, inexpensive microcontroller with built-in Wi-Fi connectivity.

The BME280 is an environmental sensor capable of measuring temperature, humidity, and atmospheric pressure.

Together, they form a simple wireless sensing node.

The idea was for the ESP8266 to read the sensor’s measurements and transmit them over my home Wi-Fi network to Home Assistant.

The wiring itself looked deceptively simple.

The BME280 communicated over I²C, a serial communication bus commonly used for connecting sensors and other peripheral devices to microcontrollers.

For my particular modules, the essential connections were:

SCL is the clock line, while SDA carries the data. The other two connections supply power and establish a common electrical ground.

Four connections.

That’s it.

I remember thinking that this should be a fairly painless undertaking.

How difficult could connecting four wires possibly be?

As it turned out, considerably more difficult than I expected.

Learning to solder for the first time

Until this project, most of my practical electronics experience had involved experimenting with components that could be connected through breadboards, jumper wires, or existing connectors.

I was comfortable enough with the underlying concepts, but soldering small electronic components was a different matter.

And now I had a collection of tiny circuit boards, header pins, wires, and a soldering iron.

I had to learn an entirely new practical skill.

At first, I underestimated the importance of the physical connection.

I experimented with inserting header pins directly into the holes on the ESP8266 and sensor boards, then attaching female jumper wires to those pins.

Mechanically, the arrangement seemed plausible. The pins were sitting in the holes, the jumper wires were attached, and the ESP8266 powered up.

Surely electricity could find its way through.

Well, electricity, as I discovered, is rather less accommodating than I’d hoped.

A metal pin sitting inside a PCB hole is not necessarily making a reliable electrical connection.

The holes are designed so that component leads or header pins can be soldered to the surrounding copper pads.

Without a proper solder joint, there may be intermittent contact, excessive resistance, or no electrical continuity at all.

So I began learning the fundamentals of soldering.

How to position a wire or header pin. How to heat the metal pad and the pin together. How to apply just enough solder to form a secure joint instead of depositing an enormous blob of molten metal.

I also had to learn what not to do.

Too much solder could accidentally bridge two neighboring connections. Too little could produce a weak joint. Moving the wire before the solder solidified could leave an unreliable connection. And holding a small PCB steady while manipulating a hot iron and solder wire required considerably more coordination than I’d anticipated.

My first attempts were hardly works of art.

There were awkward joints, messy connections, repeated inspections, lots of time when I accidentally burned my fingers, and an uncomfortable amount of uncertainty about whether I had just ruined a perfectly good circuit board.

But gradually, I started understanding the process rather than merely imitating it.

I began paying attention to the actual electrical path between the sensor and the microcontroller, not just whether the wires appeared to be attached.

This may sound trivial to someone experienced in electronics, but for me, it was an important learning experience.

I was moving from assembling components to actually understanding how to make a physical electronic system reliable.

Three ESPs, three failures, and one very annoying error message

Eventually, I connected the sensors and attempted to run them.

I configured the ESP8266 using ESPHome, flashed the firmware, and opened the device logs.

The ESP connected to Wi-Fi.

The firmware was running.

Everything looked promising.

And then:

BME280: Communication failed

The I²C scanner reported:

Found no devices

Brilliant.

I tried another ESP8266 and sensor assembly.

Same error.

I tried a third.

Same error again.

At this point, I had somehow managed to build three wireless microcontroller assemblies that could successfully connect to my network but couldn’t detect the very sensors they were supposed to monitor.

The debugging process was interesting because it forced me to separate the system into individual layers.

The ESP8266 firmware was running, so the microcontroller itself was not completely dead.

Wi-Fi worked, so the network configuration was not the main problem.

The I²C pins were configured correctly in software, but the scanner couldn’t identify any devices connected to the bus.

This narrowed the possibilities considerably.

There could have been a wiring mistake, a sensor-power problem, a bad solder joint, or a problem with the sensor module itself.

I returned to the physical connections and reworked them, paying particular attention to properly soldering the wires and headers. I removed the default male header pins that come with the ESP boards and the sensor boards and just directly cut wires and soldered each connection myself.

Then I restarted the ESP8266.

And finally, the logs showed the line I had been hoping to see:

Found device at address 0x76

The BME280 had been detected!

Moments later, real measurements started appearing:

'Room 2 Temperature' >> 24.1 °C
'Room 2 Pressure'    >> 999.8 hPa
'Room 2 Humidity'    >> 36.6 %

For the first time, an environmental sensor I had personally wired was producing measurements through firmware running on a microcontroller.

I was absurdly pleased with this. I started jumping and shouting in pure happiness!!

There is something deeply satisfying about watching a stubborn hardware project finally work after several failed attempts.

In software, many mistakes can be fixed by editing a line of code and recompiling.

Hardware is different.

Sometimes the code is entirely correct and the problem is a microscopic electrical connection that you can’t reliably diagnose by staring at a terminal.

That was a lesson I won’t forget.

5. ESPHome: Turning Homemade Electronics Into Smart-Home Devices

Now that the sensor hardware worked, I needed a reliable way to communicate its readings to my Home Assistant server.

I could have written my own firmware using Arduino libraries or another embedded development framework.

But doing so would have required me to implement and maintain the sensor communication, Wi-Fi connectivity, data reporting, and integration logic myself.

For this project, I decided to use ESPHome.

ESPHome allows you to describe the behavior of supported microcontrollers through configuration files, then generates and compiles the firmware required to run them.

Rather than write all the embedded networking code manually, I could specify the microcontroller type, Wi-Fi credentials, I²C pins, sensor model, and measurement frequency.

I self-hosted ESPHome on Buffy as another Docker service.

Its dashboard ran on port 6052, independently from the Home Assistant interface.

The workflow was relatively straightforward.

First, I connected the ESP8266 directly to Buffy over a Micro-USB cable.

The particular D1 Mini boards I purchased used a CH340 USB-to-serial interface, which allowed the computer to communicate with and program the microcontroller.

I had to make the serial device accessible to the ESPHome Docker container, since software inside a container doesn’t automatically have unrestricted access to the host’s USB hardware.

Once the connection worked, I compiled and installed the firmware.

Then I configured the BME280 component to use the I²C bus and report temperature, humidity, and pressure at approximately 30-second intervals.

Making the sensors truly wireless

Initially, I had the ESP8266 connected to Buffy through USB while testing everything.

But that wasn’t particularly useful if I wanted the sensor to sit in my bedroom.

Fortunately, USB was required only for power and initial programming, not for permanently transmitting measurements.

Once the firmware was installed, I disconnected the ESP8266 from Buffy, took it into my bedroom, and powered it using an ordinary 5V USB wall adapter.

The device booted, joined my home Wi-Fi network, and began transmitting sensor measurements.

No dedicated Raspberry Pi in the bedroom. No Ethernet cable running down the hallway. No permanent USB connection to my workstation.

Just a small microcontroller, a temperature sensor, and an ordinary wall adapter.

I added the device to Home Assistant using its ESPHome integration.

Home Assistant could then receive updates from the sensor through ESPHome’s native network API.

I repeated the arrangement for my friend’s bedroom.

And with that, I finally had all three temperature sources available through one central interface:

  1. The Honeywell thermostat in the living room, communicating through Z-Wave.

  2. An ESP8266 and BME280 in my bedroom, communicating through Wi-Fi.

  3. A second ESP8266 and BME280 in my friend’s bedroom, also communicating through Wi-Fi.

Notice that the devices weren’t even using the same wireless technology.

The thermostat used Z-Wave, while the homemade sensors used Wi-Fi.

Yet Home Assistant could combine their measurements and use them together.

This was one of the aspects of the project I found most appealing.

Different hardware, different communication protocols, one unified control system.

Actually Making the House Think: Implementing the Weighted Average

At this point, the hardware was functioning.

But merely displaying three room temperatures on a screen wasn’t going to solve the heating problem.

The whole purpose of the project was to make the system act on those measurements.

So I returned to my original weighted-average idea.

Home Assistant supports template sensors, which can calculate new values using measurements from existing devices.

I created a virtual sensor called Weighted Home Temperature.

Unlike the physical BME280 sensors, this virtual sensor didn’t correspond to a physical device.

Its measurement was calculated from the three real temperature sources using the weights I had chosen earlier:

Weighted temperature = 20% living room + 40% my bedroom + 40% friend’s bedroom.

Every time the underlying measurements changed, Home Assistant could update the calculated temperature.

The living-room measurement came from the Honeywell’s current_temperature attribute, while the bedroom readings came from their respective ESPHome sensor entities.

I also had to ensure that the temperatures were expressed in consistent units.

My ESPHome logs reported measurements in Celsius, while the Honeywell and my Home Assistant interface used Fahrenheit.

That distinction matters enormously.

A weighted average is only mathematically meaningful if the values being combined use the same scale.

Once the measurements were properly represented, I could use the weighted temperature as an input to an automation.

But I wasn’t going to make the furnace turn on whenever the average fell below exactly 69°F and turn off whenever it rose above exactly 69°F.

That would be a rather simplistic controller.

I wanted some awareness of the system’s physical behavior.

Thermal inertia and hysteresis

A house doesn’t behave like an electronic switch.

Heating systems have inertia.

Warm air takes time to circulate. Furniture and walls absorb heat. Different rooms warm at different rates. The furnace itself has operating cycles, and temperatures may continue rising even after the heating request has stopped.

If an automation repeatedly changes the thermostat setpoint in response to tiny fluctuations, it could generate unnecessary commands or unstable behavior.

This is why I introduced hysteresis.

Instead of using a single threshold, I used separate lower and upper thresholds around a desired weighted temperature.

My initial configuration used:

  • Target weighted temperature: 69°F

  • Lower threshold: 68.5°F

  • Upper threshold: 69.5°F

Below the lower threshold, the automation can request additional heating.

Above the upper threshold, it reduces the requested heating setpoint.

Between those thresholds, it generally leaves the current setpoint unchanged.

The difference between the two thresholds creates a deadband.

A small change in temperature no longer necessarily causes another thermostat adjustment.

I also configured the automation to evaluate the room temperatures every ten minutes rather than change the thermostat setpoint on every individual sensor update.

These decisions were intended to make the supervisory control logic less reactive to small fluctuations.

The Honeywell itself still manages the actual furnace cycling using its built-in temperature-control behavior.

This distinction is important because a ten-minute automation interval is not the same thing as explicitly enforcing a ten-minute minimum furnace runtime. That would require a different control mechanism, and I didn’t want to interfere with the thermostat’s own equipment-control logic.

Custom Rules: Preventing My Bedroom From Becoming a Sauna

This was the rule I cared about most. Since, obviously, it’s my own room (lol)!

Remember that my bedroom heats considerably faster than my friend’s bedroom.

Even with a weighted average, it would be possible for my room to become too warm while the colder room continued pulling the average downward.

So I added an individual-room temperature limit.

If my bedroom reaches 72°F, the automation should stop requesting additional heat, even if the weighted average is still below the target.

I implemented this as a higher-priority condition in my Home Assistant automation.

The living room also received an upper-temperature condition.

This gave the controller more nuance than a simple average-based rule.

It was no longer asking only:

Is the house, on average, too cold?

It was also asking:

Is one of the rooms( especially my own bedroom) already becoming too hot?

That second question was essential.

The colder bedroom deserved consideration, but not at the cost of overheating another occupied room.

How the thermostat is actually controlled

Home Assistant doesn’t send electricity directly to the furnace.

Instead, it uses the Z-Wave integration to request a new setpoint on the Honeywell.

For example, if the weighted temperature is low and the room limits permit heating, the automation can raise the Honeywell’s requested setpoint.

If the weighted temperature becomes sufficiently warm, or my bedroom crosses its temperature limit, the automation lowers that setpoint.

For my initial controller, I restricted the requested heating setpoints to a range of 68°F to 72°F.

When additional heat was needed, the controller used the living-room temperature as a reference, generally requesting a setpoint around two degrees above it, subject to those bounds.

This made the Honeywell more likely to call for heat while the weighted temperature remained below the target.

Conversely, when the automation wanted to reduce heating, it requested the lower setpoint of 68°F.

The actual control command was Home Assistant’s climate.set_temperature action, sent to the entity representing my living-room thermostat.

And I could verify that the command was executed.

Home Assistant provides automation traces, which record when an automation runs, which conditions are evaluated, and which actions are performed.

In one of my initial tests, I watched Home Assistant evaluate the automation and issue a setpoint command to the Honeywell.

Then I opened the thermostat’s entity state and confirmed that the setpoint had changed.

That was the final connection between the software and the physical heating equipment.

Measurements were entering the system from the rooms, the automation was evaluating those measurements, and commands were reaching the thermostat.

The feedback loop was finally connected.

An important limitation

There is a subtle but important distinction between lowering the thermostat’s setpoint and commanding the furnace to stop immediately.

Suppose my bedroom reaches 72°F while the living room is only 66°F.

If Home Assistant lowers the Honeywell’s setpoint to 68°F, the thermostat may still request heat because its own measured temperature remains below that setpoint.

In other words, my automation doesn’t have absolute control over individual rooms.

Nor should I pretend that it does.

It is a supervisory controller that modifies the thermostat’s operating target. The Honeywell remains responsible for switching the heating equipment according to its own local measurements and internal logic.

The arrangement can influence heating decisions using multiple rooms, but it cannot independently regulate airflow into each room or guarantee that one room stops heating while another continues.

Achieving that would require a more elaborate HVAC zoning solution.

For a rented house and a relatively inexpensive experiment, that would be considerable overkill.

Even by my standards.

Fail-Safes: Making Sure My Experiment Doesn’t Freeze the House

One thing I was particularly concerned about was reliability.

It’s one thing to automate a lamp. If a smart-light automation malfunctions, the worst outcome is usually an unexpectedly dark room.

Heating is rather more consequential.

What happens if one of my homemade sensors stops working?

What if a solder joint becomes unreliable?

What if Wi-Fi disconnects?

What if Buffy crashes during a machine-learning experiment or needs to reboot?

I didn’t want the basic operation of the house’s furnace to depend on my experimental software remaining perfectly functional.

So I approached the problem with a separation of responsibilities.

The Honeywell thermostat would remain the primary heating controller.

Buffy would be an additional layer of intelligence that adjusts the Honeywell’s desired temperature.

That distinction provided an important degree of independence.

The thermostat must remain functional by itself

The Honeywell T6 Pro can operate as a standalone thermostat.

Its internal temperature sensor and heating-control circuitry don’t require Home Assistant to remain online.

If Buffy goes down, the thermostat doesn’t suddenly lose the ability to operate the furnace.

This was particularly important because my workstation also runs other services and is sometimes used for computationally intensive work.

I wanted to be able to reboot it without fearing that I had disabled the house’s heating system.

However, standalone operation doesn’t automatically mean the thermostat will return to a comfortable default temperature.

If Home Assistant last commanded a 72°F setpoint, the thermostat may continue using that setpoint.

If it last commanded 68°F, it may continue using 68°F, unless an applicable local schedule changes it.

This is why I chose to keep the automated setpoints within a relatively conservative range.

Handling missing or invalid sensor measurements

In my automation, the sensor inputs are checked before calculating a heating decision.

If a measurement is unavailable, cannot be interpreted as a valid number, or falls outside a broad plausible range, the controller requests a fallback setpoint.

My initial fallback was 68°F.

The idea was to avoid allowing missing sensor values to produce nonsensical temperature calculations or extreme thermostat commands.

Of course, this only works while Home Assistant itself is running and capable of detecting the problem.

There is also a difference between a completely invalid sensor value and a plausible but inaccurate one.

A sensor that suddenly reports an impossible temperature is relatively easy to identify.

A sensor that reports 73°F when the actual temperature is 66°F is more dangerous from a software perspective because the number looks perfectly reasonable.

Detecting such problems requires more sophisticated checks, perhaps comparing readings across sensors or measuring how quickly a room’s temperature changes.

Those are worthwhile future improvements.

Restricting the commands

I also wanted to make sure my own automation wouldn’t accidentally send extreme setpoints to the thermostat.

For the initial design, I bounded its normal setpoint commands between 68°F and 72°F.

That wasn’t a complete safety system, but it limited what the experimental controller could request under ordinary conditions.

The goal was not to replace every safeguard in a commercially manufactured thermostat.

It was to enhance the thermostat without undermining its independent operation.

And because I could disable the Home Assistant automation whenever I wanted, returning to ordinary manual thermostat control remained straightforward.

My longer-term plan is to add more explicit sensor-freshness checks, monitor the controller’s decisions over time, and verify its behavior under simulated sensor and network failures.

A controller is not dependable simply because its YAML looks sensible.

The Dashboard: Seeing the Entire House at Once

Naturally, having built a multi-room heating controller, I also wanted a convenient way to observe it.

So I created a dedicated dashboard in Home Assistant.

The dashboard brings together the three physical temperature readings, the weighted average, and the Honeywell thermostat’s current operating state.

Rather than walking between rooms or checking separate applications, I could inspect everything through one interface.

This also made the system easier to debug.

If my bedroom became too warm, I could compare its temperature with the living room and my friend’s bedroom.

If the automation decided to reduce heating, I could inspect its execution trace and see which conditions were responsible.

If the thermostat wasn’t heating, I could check whether it was in Heat mode, what its current setpoint was, and whether it reported an active heating request.

The dashboard turned the system into something observable rather than a collection of hidden automations running somewhere inside my server.

And for someone interested in software engineering and autonomous systems, that observability was especially satisfying.

I was no longer merely controlling the house.

I was collecting information about its thermal behavior.

Over time, those measurements could reveal patterns in heat distribution, differences in warming and cooling rates, and the effect of changing the automation’s parameters.

In principle, the system could eventually learn which rooms respond most quickly to heating and use those observations to make better decisions.

But I wanted to establish a reliable baseline before pursuing anything more sophisticated.

Final result: Full Success !!

In the engineering sense of connecting all the components into a functioning system, yes.

I successfully installed and paired the Honeywell Z-Wave thermostat.

I connected the Zooz controller to my Ubuntu workstation and integrated it with Home Assistant.

I built wireless temperature-sensing nodes using ESP8266 microcontrollers and BME280 sensors.

I learned to solder their electrical connections, diagnosed failed I²C communication, and eventually obtained working environmental measurements.

I deployed ESPHome, configured the devices, and made their measurements available to Home Assistant over Wi-Fi.

I implemented the weighted-average temperature calculation I had originally envisioned.

And, finally, I created an automation that evaluates temperature thresholds, applies room-specific conditions, and sends actual heating setpoint commands to the Honeywell.

I was able to confirm those commands through Home Assistant’s automation traces and the thermostat’s reported state.

That’s a functional end-to-end system.

But there’s another question, and it’s an important one:

Does this actually make our house more comfortable?

I don’t honestly care, lol. All I care about is that I engineered a smart home automation and a solution to solve my own problems by taking matters into my own hands!

What I Learned From Overengineering a Thermostat

Looking back, it’s almost amusing how much this project expanded beyond its original purpose.

All I initially wanted was to stop my bedroom from getting unbearably hot whenever my roommates turned up the thermostat.

Somehow, that turned into learning about HVAC wiring, Z-Wave networking, Docker containers, embedded microcontrollers, I²C communication, soldering, Wi-Fi device integration, feedback control, hysteresis, and fault handling.

And I enjoyed practically every part of it.

Especially the failures.

There’s a particular kind of satisfaction in encountering something you don’t know how to do, learning just enough to attempt it, failing, investigating why it failed, and eventually getting it to work.

Soldering was a good example.

I could have avoided the entire difficulty by buying ready-made sensors.

But then I wouldn’t have learned how much a seemingly insignificant electrical connection matters in a real hardware system.

Similarly, I could have purchased an expensive commercial smart thermostat and accepted whatever automation capabilities it offered.

But then I wouldn’t have had the opportunity to design my own decision-making logic around the actual behavior of my house.

What appeals to me about engineering is precisely this ability to move between different layers of a problem.

A physical inconvenience becomes a sensing problem.

A sensing problem becomes a communication problem.

A communication problem becomes a software-integration problem.

And eventually, all those pieces become part of a feedback-control system that influences something in the real world.

The individual technologies I used aren’t novel.

Weighted averages have existed for centuries. Thermostats have been around for generations. Wireless environmental sensors and home-automation platforms are readily available.

The interesting part was recognizing how they could be combined to solve a very specific problem in my own environment.

And doing so myself.

Perhaps that’s the biggest lesson this project reinforced for me.

Engineering doesn’t always mean inventing something completely new. Sometimes it means refusing to accept a poorly functioning system as an unavoidable inconvenience, understanding why it behaves the way it does, and assembling the knowledge and tools required to make it better.

I started with a thermostat that knew the temperature of one room.

I ended with a locally hosted system that could observe three rooms, calculate a weighted representation of their temperatures, and use that information to influence heating decisions.

It wasn’t magic.

It was a collection of sensors, a few wires, some solder, wireless protocols, Docker containers, automation rules, and a rather unreasonable amount of curiosity.

And if there’s one thing I’ve learned, it’s that the most rewarding engineering projects aren’t necessarily the ones that begin with an elaborate research proposal or a grand technological ambition.

Sometimes they begin when you’re sitting in an overheated bedroom in the middle of a Buffalo winter, staring at an open window, and thinking:

“This is ridiculous. Surely I can engineer a better solution.”

And then you actually do.

posts.title: Why Data Collection is extremely important for cutting-edge research... and how it looks like
posts.summary: Behind every dataset, every experiment, and every impressive robotics demonstration is a considerable amount of work that rarely makes it into the final research paper.
posts.html:
When we think about research in artificial intelligence and robotics, we usually imagine sophisticated algorithms, mathematical formulations, neural networks, experimental results, and perhaps a robot performing some remarkable task.

We rarely imagine someone spending hours walking a robot through the same hallway, figuring out which direction to approach a corner from, carrying heavy batteries and equipment between locations, or deciding whether a particular lighting condition is actually worth recording.

And yet, a surprising amount of research, sometimes even exciting research methods, happens precisely there.

I’ve been experiencing this firsthand while working on the Active Illumination research project involving Boston Dynamics’ Spot robot at the University at Buffalo’s Drones Lab, under the mentorship of Yash Turkar.

A significant part of my work involves collecting visual data and designing capture sequences in real-world environments. This sounds straightforward on paper. In practice, however, it has given me a completely different appreciation for what goes into producing a useful research dataset.

1. Active Illumination : See, Predict, Act

A mobile robot equipped with a programmable co-located camera-light system. https://droneslab.github.io/LGTN

Robots often need to navigate places where vision is least reliable: dark corridors, reflective interiors, tunnels, and abrupt indoor-outdoor transitions. A passive camera can only process the light already available. Simply turning a lamp to maximum power is not a complete solution either; too much light can create glare, saturation, reflections, and wasted energy. Active illumination treats the robot’s light as part of the sensing system, something the robot can control intelligently to reveal useful structure while avoiding new perception failures

The central question of this project is: How can a robot decide how to illuminate the world, predict what it will see, and select lighting actions that improve perception?

This is a very interesting research question that fascinates me. A fully autonomous robot is literally being tasked to explore some unknown, dark location on its own with no prior knowledge of the environment. It could encounter unforseen obstacles, potential damages to its own body and the onboard computer and cameras. It must carefully tread by illuminating its path in front of it, while keeping in mind that too much light can screw up its own camera readings, and too less light would also result in it not seeing something and accidentally smashing.

To train such a model, a lot of data collection is needed. And this isn’t something as simple as how commonplace LLMs behind ChatGPT are trained: there is no automated web scraping, no tokenization involving billions of text files to be used as data for training some model.

Instead, the data is very real: the paths we walk at night, dark corridors, rooms, halls, culverts, etc: real-world, with many new variables involved.

2. The Part of Research Nobody Really Sees

A research paper might describe its experimental setup in a paragraph:

“We collected sequences across multiple indoor environments under varying illumination conditions.”

But behind that sentence could be hours of preparation, repeated walks through the same environment, equipment transportation, battery management, troubleshooting, and careful decisions about which sequences are scientifically useful.

Working with Spot makes this particularly apparent.

Unlike downloading a dataset or running a simulation, real-world data collection requires physically interacting with the environment. The robot has to be prepared, equipment has to be transported, suitable locations must be identified, and each sequence needs to serve a purpose.

Given the nature of such data collection, in which the environment has to be outside a lab, but also with no people around ( having someone come in our camera-captured photos and videos would not make much sense for training a fully autonomous robot meant to navigate dark culverts on its own), this naturally requires us to collect data sequences late at night , sometimes staying up till even 6 AM, when there is no one around in rooms, corridors, and campus areas in the university. Which makes it even more fun and hands-on than working with purely software!

Sometimes, a considerable amount of effort goes into collecting what appears to be a rather unremarkable sequence: a robot walking down a corridor.

But the difficulty isn’t necessarily in getting the robot from point A to point B.

It’s in determining what that journey can teach us.

A recording of Spot walking down a hallway is just a recording until we can explain why that hallway, why that trajectory, why those lighting conditions, and what scientific question the sequence helps answer.

That’s where data collection starts becoming research.

Consider the following photo:

This features a secluded, dark room in a library with a narrow path ahead, with desks on one side and book shelves on the other. Now, in a fully dark room with no light, a fully autonomous Spot robot could be tasked with navigating it for some objective( say, an earthquake hit a building and Search-and-Rescue is needed to save lives, but it is too risky for helpers to go inside such a dark building, so they send Spot to assess the situation inside). Now, if Spot turns the headlights to 100% brightness to see with its co-located cameras, the light might fully reflect off of a smooth table, chair, or a reflective glass pane, and Spot might get confused with the reflection, panick, and smash itself ! Contrary to this scenario, if Spot reduces its brightness too much , it might mistake objects in the dark ( just like humans do) and still smash into something, thereby risking $100k worth of its own robot body! Clearly, there needs to be some intelligent, learned behaviour to adaptively control the level of brightness of its own headlights, to match its vision in real-time. This prediction( predicting the future state, or level of brightness) also needs to be very fast and accurate, giving Spot enough time to change its action.

A huge part of the data collection process involves facing Spot towards objects, such as this book shelf, in varying levels of illumination in the room, sometimes dark, sometimes medium, sometimes fully lit, and at different angles facing an object, in order to capture high-quality and varying data so that all kinds of materials ( with different reflective properties) are adequately captured.

What appears to be a simple bookshelf actually presents an interesting experimental setting. Books, shelves, and surrounding objects have different surface textures, colors, and reflective properties, each interacting with light differently. By varying Spot’s viewing angle, distance, and illumination conditions, we can observe how shadows, reflections, highlights, and visible surface details change across images.

The challenge isn’t simply to record an object from as many angles as possible. It’s to design sequences that introduce meaningful variations while preserving enough consistency to make comparisons useful. Even a small change in viewpoint or illumination can affect which visual features remain observable.

And that’s one of the things I’ve come to appreciate about this work: a seemingly ordinary bookshelf can become a carefully chosen experimental scene when you begin thinking about it through the lens of robotic perception.

So the answer isn’t simply to turn the lights on or off. The robot needs to understand how much illumination is useful, where it is useful, and when to adjust it.

The Need for Intelligent, Adaptive Illumination

This is where the problem starts becoming particularly interesting from an artificial intelligence perspective.

Ideally, a robot should be able to evaluate its current visual observations, recognize when illumination is inadequate or excessive, and adapt its lighting accordingly.

And because the robot is continuously moving, making decisions based only on its current image may not always be sufficient.

It may also be valuable to anticipate what happens next.

For example, if Spot is approaching a highly reflective surface, it could potentially predict that maintaining its present illumination level will produce glare as its viewpoint changes. Similarly, when entering a darker region, it could anticipate the need for additional lighting before visual information deteriorates significantly.

Such a system could learn a policy that maps observations and robot state to suitable lighting actions, potentially accounting for camera exposure, motion, scene geometry, and the location of reflective surfaces.

The objective is not necessarily to maximize image brightness.

It is to maximize the usefulness of the visual information available to the robot.

There is also the question of time. A decision that arrives too late may be of little use. If a mobile robot is approaching an obstacle, its perception and control pipeline must operate quickly enough for the illumination adjustment to improve observations before those observations are needed for navigation.

A practical system therefore needs to balance perception quality, computation time, illumination response, power consumption, and safe robot behavior.

This is a much more challenging problem than simply choosing between a few brightness settings.

But How Would We Teach a Robot to Do This?

And this brings us back to data collection.

How can we expect an algorithm to learn which illumination conditions are useful if we have never observed how different scenes respond to different levels of light?

How can it learn to distinguish a dim, textured wall from a reflective surface that becomes saturated under strong illumination?

How can we evaluate whether a lighting strategy works across different environments without collecting observations from those environments?

We need data. Not just enormous quantities of arbitrary images, but carefully designed sequences that expose the system to meaningful variations in the physical world.

This is why, during our data collection sessions, we spend time positioning Spot in front of different objects, observing them from different angles, and recording scenes under varying illumination conditions.

A bookshelf, for instance, is not simply a bookshelf from the perspective of an experiment. It contains surfaces with different colors, textures, orientations, and reflective characteristics. A glossy book cover may interact with light differently from matte paper. A smooth tabletop may produce a bright highlight, while a textured fabric chair scatters light differently. A dark surface might reflect little visible light into the camera despite being close to the robot. Even within the same scene, changing the robot’s orientation can change the image dramatically.

And this is precisely why collecting a single recording under a single lighting condition would be insufficient for studying illumination-dependent visual perception.

We need to ask:

  • What happens when the same object is observed under low, medium, and high illumination?

  • What changes when Spot approaches the object from a different direction?

  • Which surface features become visible or disappear as the lighting changes?

  • At what point does additional illumination stop helping and begin degrading image quality?

  • Can we identify conditions under which different illumination choices consistently improve useful visual observations?

These questions guide the selection of our capture sequences.

For a scientifically meaningful comparison, we also need to think carefully about controlling other variables. If the robot moves to a completely different location every time we change the brightness, we may struggle to determine whether a change in image quality was caused by the illumination or by the environment itself.

Repeated trajectories, consistent viewpoints, synchronized sensor measurements, and recorded illumination settings can therefore be just as valuable as collecting entirely new scenes.

The quality of a dataset is determined not only by how much diversity it contains, but also by whether its observations allow us to investigate the questions we care about.

Why Hours of Repetition Matter

Now imagine doing this not for one object, but for dozens of different environments and geometric configurations.

A narrow hallway. A dark corner. A reflective table. A room with large glass windows. A set of bookshelves. A staircase. A passage illuminated from one side.

Each environment introduces different challenges.

And within every environment, we can vary the robot’s viewpoint, path, distance, and lighting.

This produces a considerable number of possible experimental combinations.

Of course, collecting every possible combination is neither practical nor necessary.
