Part of the researcher’s responsibility is deciding which observations are likely to be informative, which conditions are underrepresented, and which experiments would help distinguish between competing explanations.

That means a lot of walking.

A lot of repositioning Spot.

A lot of setting up equipment, carrying batteries, planning paths, and repeating sequences that might appear almost identical to an outside observer.

Sometimes, much of this happens late at night, when the university building is nearly empty and the environment is easier to use for controlled recordings.

To somebody unfamiliar with the research, it might look like hours spent making an expensive robot walk around a library.

however, we’re systematically observing how the physical world presents itself to a robotic perception system, and gathering the evidence needed to make that perception more reliable.

A learning algorithm can only learn from the experiences and signals made available to it. If our dataset contains only clean, brightly illuminated scenes, we cannot simply assume that a system trained or evaluated on it will behave reliably in dark, reflective, cluttered, or unfamiliar environments.

And collecting diverse data is not, by itself, a guarantee of generalization. We still need rigorous experiments, appropriate evaluations, and testing on conditions the system has not already encountered.

But without representative, carefully collected data, even an exceptionally sophisticated learning algorithm may have little basis for understanding the conditions we expect it to handle. That’s why data collection deserves so much more attention than it usually receives.

Because long before a robot can learn how to respond intelligently to a difficult environment, somebody has to go out into the physical world, find those difficulties, design ways to observe them, and collect the evidence.

And sometimes, that means spending hours walking a yellow quadruped through a dark, empty library, because we’re trying to understand how to help it perceive the world well enough to navigate the unknown.

3. Why I Keep Coming Back

A little while ago, I was describing my work at the lab to a classmate: the hours spent collecting sequences, walking Spot through buildings, carrying batteries and equipment around, and the sheer amount of time that goes into preparing what might eventually become just a small part of a research experiment.

His response was interesting.

He asked me, essentially, why I was still doing all of this.

We’re both international students approaching graduation, trying to navigate an uncertain job market. And from his perspective, the calculation was fairly straightforward. This was an unpaid research position. I had already spent enough time at the lab to have something meaningful to put on my résumé. Why continue spending so many hours every week when I could be using that time to prepare for interviews, apply for jobs, or work on something with a more immediate return?

He wasn’t necessarily wrong.

In fact, from a purely practical standpoint, his reasoning made a lot of sense. Time is limited, especially when you’re about to graduate and looking for employment. And there’s nothing unreasonable about wanting your work to translate into something tangible.

I didn’t have much of a response for him at the time.

But I think I know what I would say now.

I do it because I love it.

Not because I’m guaranteed a publication. Not because I’m being paid. Not because I need another bullet point on my résumé.

I genuinely enjoy the research. I enjoy the engineering challenges, the experiments, and even the seemingly mundane work that goes into making those experiments possible. Even something as simple as getting a chance to walk Spot around one more time is enough to make me happy.

There’s something deeply satisfying about walking through a nearly empty university building late at night, with Spot beside me, thinking about what sequence to capture next. Wondering whether a particular corridor would make an interesting experiment. Whether changing the lighting would reveal something we hadn’t observed before. Whether a different trajectory could produce more useful data.

Sometimes it’s exhausting. Sometimes it’s repetitive. Sometimes, after hours of work, the visible progress seems disproportionately small compared to the effort involved.

But I still find myself wanting to come back and do it again.

Because to me, research isn’t just the final paper, the successful demonstration, or the result that eventually makes its way into a presentation.

It’s also the process of asking questions, designing experiments, building things, making mistakes, and gradually understanding something that you didn’t understand before.

And I think that’s what my friend and I were looking at differently.

He was evaluating the work primarily in terms of what it could give him afterward.

I was finding value in the work itself.

That doesn’t mean compensation doesn’t matter, or that everyone should be expected to work for free. It certainly doesn’t mean that passion alone makes unpaid labor fair or sustainable. I recognize that I’m fortunate to be in a position where I can choose to devote some of my time to this research.

But for me, at this particular stage of my life, it’s a choice I’m happy to make.

I don’t know exactly what this project will lead to. Perhaps a publication, perhaps a new research direction, perhaps simply a deeper understanding of robotic perception and experimental methodology.

What I do know is that every time I find myself planning a new experiment, figuring out how to collect better data, or solving an unexpected technical problem, I’m reminded of why I became interested in engineering in the first place.

The process itself awakens the engineer in me.

And sometimes, that’s enough of a reason to keep going.

PS: Huge thanks to Shouvik Das for being a great help to me always, your friendly attitude makes long data collecting sessions like these a lot more fun!

Huge thanks to PhD candidate Yash Turkar for giving me an opportunity to join your research project as your student research assistant!

posts.title: How I Turned My Campus Job Into an Optimization Problem
posts.summary: Solving an optimization problem in my real-world life scenario
posts.html:
I work part-time for an on-campus job while completing my masters from my university. The work shifts are usually 15 hours a week, or 5 hours per shift, and consist of working at dining stations which prepare and serve food. These shifts are usually brutal, physically demanding, very repetitive, and quickly drain your energy and time. During these shifts, it is very hard to tolerate the excrutiatingly slow passage of time, when all you’re wondering is when will your shift be finally over. All we’re forced to do is physical work: no mental/ intellectual stimulation happens, so we’re forced to pass time working/ making small talks and conversations with colleagues. So, to pass time better, I set forth to spend my time thinking while working. Thinking, particularly, on a very interesting problem. And I’ve had great pleasure in solving this problem systematically.

During these shifts, one of my responsibilities is managing the beverage stations. On paper, the job is simple: make sure there are always enough clean glasses available. In practice, this means constantly moving crates of glasses, collecting empty crates, transporting them back to the dish room, bringing out freshly filled ones, and making sure neither of the two beverage stations runs out during a rush. Specifically, there are two main beverage stations, which I’ll simply call the Front Station and the Back Station. Each station has a Primary cart containing roughly five to six crates stacked on top of one another. These are the glasses customers actually take from. Next to it is a cart for collecting empty crates ( the empty stack), along with a Backup cart containing additional crates filled with clean glasses.

As customers take glasses, the top crate gradually empties. Once empty, I move it to the empty-crate cart, exposing the next crate underneath. I can then either let the primary stack continue shrinking, replenish it using crates from the backup cart, reorganize the stacks, or make a trip to the dish room: taking empty crates in and returning with a newly filled cart.

After doing this for a while, I started noticing something: I was solving an optimization problem without treating it like one. Each of the choices seems trivial in isolation. Over a five-hour shift, however, they add up. More importantly, they do not all have the same cost. Moving an empty crate takes almost no effort. Moving a crate full of glasses does. Moving that same full crate from waist height is relatively easy; moving it from the top of a five-foot stack is considerably more physically demanding. A trip to the dish room costs time, but it can also replace several individual crate movements at once.

And of course, there is one hard constraint: the customers should never run out of glasses.

So instead of asking, “How do I keep these stations filled?”, I started asking a much more interesting question:

What sequence of actions minimizes the total amount of work I have to do over a five-hour shift, while guaranteeing that both stations remain supplied? Here, work/effort is directly proportional to my physical energy, and my back muscles which are getting strained while lifting heavy crates. So, obviously, it is in my best interest to solve this problem optimally.

Suddenly, my annoying part-time job looked a lot like a computer science problem.

Turning Effort Into a Cost Function

The first step was deciding what I was actually trying to optimize.

The obvious answer was effort, but effort is not a single quantity. Carrying an empty crate and carrying a crate filled with glasses are technically the same action, yet they feel nothing alike. Similarly, moving a full crate from waist height is considerably easier than pulling one from near, or greater than, my shoulder height. Walking to the dish room costs relatively little physical effort, but doing it unnecessarily ten times during a shift still adds up.

So I broke the problem into a few variables. I quickly set forth to collect useful data points during a day shift with average rush ( during peak rush hours, since different number of people come at different times during the evenings, I averaged out my variables across all hours of my shift): timestamps of each emptied crate at both stations, number of crates on each cart, dish-room round-trip time, and roughly how long each full-crate transfer takes me.

The observations: [time to finish 1 crate in back beverage station( at the top of primary cart) was 6 minutes. Time for whole primary stack to finish was 30 minutes, so every 30 minutes a new stack comes out from dish room. Same goes for front station. Number of crates on primary carts equals 5-6 on average. backup carts have crates more than , or sometimes equal to, the primary carts. dish room round trip time takes 1-2 minutes. each full-crate transfer takes negligible time, but more physical effort as expected.]

With my initial observations, I solved this problem which presented to me as an amazing online stochastic optimization problem. It is a beautiful mixture:

Online, because I don’t know exactly when students will arrive.

Stochastic, because glass consumption varies randomly.

Inventory control, because I’m deciding how much stock to maintain at each station.

Vehicle/inventory routing, because I’m transporting inventory between dish and multiple consumption points.

Scheduling, because two stations compete for my attention.

Batching, because combining several replenishment needs into one trip reduces fixed costs.

Bin packing / consolidation, loosely, when I’m rearranging glasses between partially occupied crates.

And there’s even a robotics analogy: if I replaced myself with a mobile robot tasked with maintaining both stations, this would look like a small task-and-motion planning / pickup-and-delivery problem with inventory constraints.

Now, initially I estimated that my effort was directly proprotional to the max height of the backup crate from where I would pick fully-filled cart of glasses and carry it and drop it on the recently-finished stack top from the Primary Cart, and so the effort was a product of a few factors:

Factor 1: lifting a fully filled crate from the pile of glasses to the primary crate stack takes my energy and causes strain on my muscles.

Factor 2: this effort is directly proportional to the duration for which I have to hold and move the crate, as well as the original height of the stack from which I took it( as it’s easier for me to lift a heavy crate from below my height rather than moving a crate close to or greater than my height, which is 5 foot 7).

Factor 3: the number of times I have to switch the crates to fill the dwindling stack, shuffle empty slots with glasses from another crate stack to reduce the weight of future crate movements, and the number of times I have to visit dish room by taking empty crates stacks and coming out with fresh,new heavy stacked crates full of new glasses. These factors are directly proportional to my efforts, so they can be represented as a product.

But here is when ChatGPT pointed out my mistake, and suggested to me that it would be more accurate if I instead took into account the square of the height difference between my height, and the max height of any cart( lesser or greater in height than me).

ChatGPT suggested me that the the key insight is that a crate movement does not have a constant cost. Moving a full crate 1 meter at waist height is very different from lifting one from the top of a ~5’3” stack, carrying it several meters, and placing it somewhere else. On top of that, I have inventory depletion, replenishment trips, two beverage stations, and the option to partially redistribute glasses between crates.

The following is what ChatGPT said about my problem:

Model what you're actually minimizing
I would not multiply all your factors together directly. That produces weird behavior: for example, if one factor becomes nearly zero, the entire cost becomes nearly zero regardless of the others.
Instead, give every action a cost.
For moving crate i:

So, given this advice, I set to implement my next day’s shift with these rules in mind:

  1. Never let the working (Primary) stack fall below 2 crates without already having replenishment immediately available.

  2. Avoid building unnecessarily tall towers of full crates. Keep heavy reserve inventory primarily within your comfortable lifting zone when workplace rules and available space permit.[ I used to do this a lot, to help my future-lazy self, but now I realize that I was in fact making my job harder]

  3. Batch dish-room trips across both beverage stations. Before leaving, inspect both stations and take as many empties as practical; return with enough clean crates to cover both until your next expected trip.

  4. Only redistribute glasses when it eliminates a future heavy-crate movement or frees a crate. Don’t reorganize for neatness.

So instead of:

empty → replace → empty → replace → dish → return → rearrange → replace...

I implemented a new strategy:

consume → accumulate → consolidate when worthwhile → batch → replenish → consume

With my newly collected data points in mind, this is how I solved this problem:

The dominant cost is not walking/time. It was simply my unnecessary manipulation of full crates, especially at bad heights.

My measured demand rate per station is approximately

so over a 5-hour shift:

or roughly 100 crate-equivalents of glasses consumed across both stations on a medium-demand shift. A 5-crate primary lasts ~30 min; a 6-crate primary should last ~36 min, so this confirms that my observations are internally consistent.

The most important result

My dish-room round trips last only 1–2 minutes, while one crate lasts ~6 minutes.

So during even the worst 2-minute trip, a station consumes only: 0.33 crates on average ( or 1/3rd of a full crate, which is around 8 glasses)

So one full crate represents 3× the maximum inventory I need merely to survive a dish-room trip.

That means having 5–6 crates on the primary plus another 5–6+ full crates on the backup cart is far more local inventory than I ever need from a replenishment-risk perspective. The backup wasn’t really protecting me from stockout. It was always mainly creating a large buffer.

This was my biggest mistake, and I quickly stopped doing this after I solved this optimization problem.

The final optimal solution is this: Use cart rotation.

Suppose:

Primary: 5 full crates

Backup: 5–6 full crates

Empty cart: accumulating empties

Let Primary run almost all the way down.

So I’ve changed the fundamental operation from:

lift full crate → carry → place → repeat

to:

roll cart → roll cart → roll cart

That’s an enormous optimization because wheels substitute rolling work for loaded lifting!

PS: There’s a funny plot twist to this story. While I took the route of the algorithmic solver, thinking of all possible ways to optimize this problem logically, one of my work colleagues, an undergrad guy, told me he had already solved this problem himself a long time ago, and minimized his effort the best way possible: by slacking off his assigned job, cutting corners, and disappearing from his station during peak rush hours so that our managers/ student leaders are forced to do all the crate emptying/ replacing themselves! This shocked me so much that I simply burst out laughing!

posts.title: Why OnlyFans sells more than Gold’s Gym ?
posts.summary: You’ll see people spend instantly on food delivery, gadgets, Netflix, or even porn apps like OnlyFans.
posts.html:
You’ll see people spend instantly on food delivery, gadgets, Netflix, or even porn apps like OnlyFans. Everyday people consume products and experiences that boost their dopamine rush. Sugar-filled coffees, malls, clothes, restaurants,etc.

But then the same people will hesitate to buy a gym membership, a discipline app, learning resources like Duolingo or coding bootcamps, some product that requires them to take physical or mental efforts, or basically anything that promises long-term self-growth.

People crave dopamine everyday. That is just human. No one can change our behaviour. That is why, products that boost our dopamine or increase our comfort zone will always be much, much more profitable as a business.

This is a reminder for tech founders, or basically anyone brave enough to launch their own product/service. Often, we become too wrapped in our own engineering delusions, such that we overcomplicate our product offerings. We always aim to innovate, spend countless hours programming a new unique app feature to stand out. We may tell users that our app has some powerful back-end solution, or a new AI model, or a new cloud service, etc. It doesn’t matter. No one cares. I have realized this now, after spending many days in trial and error. Too much energy is spent in thinking about what others ( our “possible” customers in some distant future) may like in our product. When the simple solution is : just make something that increases dopamine rush in people. That’s it. Dead simple.

Nowadays, you’ll find many new tech founders spend countless months making some app ( with crazy complicated backend, APIs, cloud solutions, excessive features, etc) that frankly no one cares about. The only thing the user cares about is his time and comfort. If you present someone a new interface, they won’t care about how some AI handles their needs. All they care about is fast results that increase their comfort and make them do so with as little clicks as possible, and as little effort taken as possible.

Believe me, I’ve personally gone through this hell. Alone. Many times. I’ve faced utter failures. No one cared about my apps. No one responded to my marketing on social media. Even today, when I visit Youtube, Twitter or Instagram, I come across new tech startups that fail to see this simple picture. They overcomplicate stuff by saying “decentralized governance”, “ smart contracts” , “Multi Context protocol”, “fine-tuned LLMs”, and other jargon , instead of simply saying: “this app will help you write emails faster”.

Again :

More complex = More efforts on behalf of users = less purchases = less business.

With new innovations in AI following ChatGPT and LLMs , people have forgotten to keep it simple anymore. Overcomplicating stuff in product apps that’s meant only for research papers or technological progress. It’s a really bad idea to mix complicated code or architecture in your project if it doesn’t provide a 10x improvement to users over the apps they currently use.

For example, the reason why ChatGPT is the fastest growing app across all platforms is not because Sam Altman markets its underlying LLM architecture, but because it feels “magical” : it’s response time is amazing, its chat interface works beautifully, and it’s very useful for everyone. Instant dopamine rush. Instant comfort. More comfort added to a person’s hand. And yet there are many new startups attempting to create better versions of such versions without truly understanding this simple reason behind its success.

Once someone interested in entrepreneurship becomes a computer engineer, or graduates from a technical college course , the natural tendency of that person is to build a new app that can be turned into a profitable business by applying the interesting concepts he learned. However unless his app provides a 10x improvement over existing competition, it will naturally fail( as observed by Peter Thiel himself too). If that app doesn’t provide instant dopamine rush to the common public, it might still be decently sold, but nowhere near the success that profitable businesses get.

There’s no shame in a non-tech or traditional business. If you’re a ML engineer or a software dev broadly speaking, why limit yourself to only making money via coding? If you’re solely interested in only business, why not pursue a normal business plan with a proven success record, such as setting up a cafe, or pursuing business in finance, healthcare, real estate, content creation on Youtube, etc ?

I’m not against innovation. But let’s be real. Probability wise, the chances that your “new agentic AI app” or “decentralized smart energy system” becomes the next iPhone is less than 1%. Entrepreneurship is all about risks. More risks, more rewards. But building in the direction of something that’s never been done before, in a field such as AI which is still in its infant stage, is stupid. How do you expect to compete with other companies like Google or OpenAI who are spending billions of dollars on AI innovations by hiring top scientists and AI engineers? Better spend your energy on something that’s very profitable, with higher chances of success and which gives you higher chances of crushing your opponents in the market : like selling new t-shirts with creative designs, or opening a new cafe/club, or making simple mobile apps in a market with a long history, proven success rate, proven user base, and proven profitability.

A student will quickly buy a new Macbook or pay for an app like Netflix , because it increases their social status, novelty sense, and gives them the dopamine rush. They won’t even care to buy a paid subscription to some new startup’s “AI-powered code editor” or some other glorified frontend that simply uses APIs of other companies, because that student can simply get all that for free forever with chatgpt ( and its responsive fast cloud servers).

I’m not saying that such products never get sold. Of course not. Many people use discipline apps like NoFap, meditation services, fitness apps, and much more.

I myself built a calorie tracker mobile app as a direct competitor to CalAI and Myfitnesspal, apps that have made millions in revenue. But compared to dopamine-inducing businesses like McDonald’s or Starbucks or Coca-Cola? They fall far behind, pale in comparison. If tomorrow I set to make a gambling app instead of a fitness app, it will definitely sell much better. Maybe that’s what I should do next time , lol. Build something dopamine-inducing.

Case in point: Businesses that sell quickly consumable products that increase comfort and dopamine for people sell much better than those who don’t. There’s no shame in pursuing a traditional business like printing t-shirts, opening coffee shops, owning a restaurant, etc, even if you come from a technical background like a ML engineer or a software developer. When it comes to entrepreneurship, anything that makes money is a business. Simple as that. You can easily quench your thirst for pursuing innovation and new scientific discoveries without mixing them up with business ideas. You could even invent a new AI architecture, without having to turn every idea into something “could” one day become a business, but you’ll have to suffer a lot: spend countless time and energy( half your life, all of your youth) alone. It’s not worth the effort. Steve Jobs got lucky as he had a genius with him : Steve Wozniak. So did others. They got lucky. Really lucky. What if you risk it all for nothing? No hope for a successful career. That’s just wishful I’m not talking against entrepreneurship. I’m talking against pursuing entrepreneurship in a niche that’s almost impossible to crack , like pursuing competition with top AI companies, of building a new OS to challenge Linux or Windows. I’m talking about pursuing entrepreneurship in a market with a proven long history and a success record for other businesses: real estate, finance, food, entertainment etc.

In the rush to avoid a 9-5 job , many young people risk a lot to become an entrepreneur, and focus on the wrong things. Entrepreneurship is the best: but only if you follow a smart option , build a product that people will greedily buy , rather than building some scientific contraption that no one will buy.

In conclusion: build products that are lucrative and attractive to many people( could be a niche: like sports shoes, but still: it must become a sensation) . Stick to the basics. Keep it simple.

posts.title: EP.1 Kaggle is the BEST for ML engineers who don’t have local GPUs ?
posts.summary: Sesame AI becomes the best conversational AI, and Kaggle reigns supreme for ML engineers....
posts.html:
Meet the latest best conversational AI : Sesame

Sesame AI

Talk with an AI-generated voice for as much time as you want! It shows amazing performance across a wide range of parameters such as how much it understands our conversation, the “emotions” it can convey via its voice expressions, and its ability to show “surprise”, or show patience whenever it is interrupted. It will blow your mind, I promise.

Thanks for reading The Algorithmic Investigator! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.

The research team at Sesame have open-sourced their technical work( thanks a lot to the team!). In it, they describe how they have innovated in this domain. Traditionally, AI for speech tasks employ a TTS( text to speech) pipeline but this has limitations because it is a form of generative AI that only generates the next tokens without having “context awareness”. To address this, they introduce a new model called CSM (Conversational speech model) designed to be a multimodal model ( text and audio). They use 2 transformers ( variants of the Llama architecture), and a different method of handling audio input tokens( instead of traditionally used methods of semantic and acoustic tokens). They customize the AI model’s modules to introduce many more training and inference efficiences as well. Refer to their technical report in the above link to learn more.

This demonstrates the power and rapid growth of open-source models and progressive AI startups. Try Sesame out today !

Why I transitioned to Kaggle as a ML engineer

As a ML engineer, I always have to write code for the following things :

  • importing and handling datasets.

  • Cleaning dataset & converting it into relevant a dataframe.

  • Making sure only useful features are present, and unnecessary values are removed. Making sure those values are normalized so that they won’t cause me problems later

  • Building models with Pytorch: creating a dataset template, then splitting it across a test and a train data loader. Then, importing and customizing a model according to my end goals.

  • Then finally, hitting the start button to run the training loop for my model ( for some number of epochs).

However, this last step ( while fun to watch the progress bar of your model being trained per epoch, and your loss values steadily dropping) causes some issues. This is because I do not have my own GPU where I can train AI models efficiently. My projects would require something as powerful as an Nvidia RTX 4090. The only choice remaining for AI engineers like me is to use online notebooks or VM instances. Specifically, the choice of your training environment matters a lot.

Google Colab is probably the most popularly used by ML engineers for this purpose. I Under their free tier, they provide access to normal CPU, and a T4 GPU. This T4 GPU is very powerful, sometimes exceeding average Nvidia GPUs due to the presence of Tensor Cores, which allows for fast parallel processing of your tensors in your Pytorch( or tensorflow) code, during the training/model learning phase.

However, Google Colab has a serious flaw : If you keep the model training on, and wait for a long time until it does its thing, Colab automatically shuts down your notebook instance, even if you keep your tab or screen open, and even if you are completely active on screen, whether you keep moving your mouse cursor,etc !

This is a serious problem because you cannot keep on waiting, staring at the screen forever, as the model training takes up to 4-5 hours or more ! Along with this, another common problem of Colab is this :

Clearly, we need a better alternative to this. Some solutions exist, such as PaperSpace, but I have found something much better: Kaggle notebooks. In hindsight, I should have known this much earlier, but I am honestly surprised how very few people know about it.

It has some amazing advantages over common alternatives, such as:

You can make your files and variables persistent ( so that your progress is not lost):

But by far, the best feature offered by Kaggle is this :

Notice how it says T4 x 2 ?! You read it right ! Under their free tier, they offer up to 30 hours of continous GPU usage across two T4 GPUs per week ! This is clearly much better than other free alternatives. ML engineers can use these GPUs at the same time for training their models, using a simple Pytorch function : model = nn.DataParallel(model). This code line allows them to parallelize the model training to fully exploit the power of 2 GPUs at the same time !

Oh, and did I mention that you can trigger your Kaggle notebook to run at a set time ? You can schedule your notebook to run automatically, even if,say, you are sleeping! DevOps philosophy at its peak !

Not to mention that Kaggle has probably the best ecosystem when it comes to public datasets, model competitions and amazing incentives for ML project makers such as giving them badges for completing a task or acheiving a milestone ! Kaggle is the best starting point for all data scientists and ML engineers.

So wait no more, transition your workflow for your ML projects to Kaggle today itself!

Thanks for reading The Algorithmic Investigator! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.

posts.title: American Capitalism Part 2 : The insidious nature of MNCs and the dual-edged sword of monopolization.
posts.summary: How some large corporations,top execs, and government policies inhibit innovation, affect economy, and go against the true nature of capitalism.
posts.html:
There are only two highly effective ways to grow wealth quickly and exponentially: you either own something that grows in value over time as an investor or an asset manager, or you build something innovative and sell it to a growing market with lots of demand by building a business around what you are selling(entrepreneurship), and owning a stake in your own business that grows in value. Both of these approaches are highly risky, where in 9 out of 10 cases you will most certainly fail. The high risk you take is what deems you worthy of receiving exponential capital gains in the future. You can be a stock trader that invests in high-risk assets and earn a lot of money by simply owning something of value, or you make something new and sell it to a market as a “builder”.

My last article on this subject elaborated a lot on this topic, and how exactly American capitalism works. The American Dream is enabled by such capitalistic spirit: that any person ,regardless of his genetics, color, country of origin, race, religion, can live in the USA, reinventt himself, and take advantage of capitalism to achieve true freedom. Such a system cannot be seen in any other country by far. The opposing philosophies to capitalism are socialism, communism, etc, and they have all miserably failed. Only the USA has prevailed for more than 2 centuries.

This however, works hand-in-hand with the government policies of a country. We must carefully understand how countries operate because the government policies are what enable the operations of corporations and startups. In a way, government affects the world economy, which in turn affects entrepreneurs and investors. Particularly in the USA, capitalism experiences limited interference by the government. The free market system ensures that corporations such as private/public companies and startups run by entrepreneurs and corporate executives take care of all of the country’s growth, innovation, and economy. Corporations need to always raise money to reinvest in themselves to accelerate their further growth, which drives more job creation, more inventions, more progress. They raise this money in an environment of low interest rates, where less rates implies greater loans that can be easily taken from banks or other institutions. In a period of recession or inflation, interest rates rise as well, making it more expensive and harder for corporations to receive loans. This is how every industry works, in any decade from our history, where corporations drive the growth of the economy, and the rate at which they can grow is dependent upon the current market conditions and the overall health of the economy. This is seen not just for banks, but also for any other methods of raising money from investors, such as Venture Capital firms or private equity firms, where the willingness of lending money depends on the mindset of the limited partners, which in turn depends on the current economy health. The other way corporations raise money is by going public, and receiving a public market cap on their business, where the public can invest in their buiness through a stock exchange. This however, implies an exit on the side of the original founders, execs, and the board. A new board then replaces the previous one, or in rare cases, the CEO retains his position for a long time.

The monetary and fiscal policies of a government must then operate in sync with this free market system. The monetary policy implies that a central bank, the Federal Reserve, takes care of new money printing in Washington, controlling interest rates and monitoring inflation carefully. The fiscal policy implies how the government spends its money and its tax policies. Two notable philosophies are at play here: Keynesian economics, as proposed by the famous economist John Maynard Keynes in the 1930s, and Friedmanite economics, as proposed by the famous economist Milton Friedman in the 1970s and 1980s. Keynesian economics is adopted by fiscal policies, where the government intervenes inside the free market system to propose taxations, regulation, government spending on infrastructure, and so on. Whereas the Friedmanite economics focuses on the hyper-capitalist mentality : increasing profits is the sole purpose of a business, where it benefits all stakeholders and creates more jobs, drives further economy, and encourages free-trade systems between different countries. Friendman suggests that there should be a reduction in government interference and there should be more tax cuts, and also argued that the real reason why inflation occurs only when there is more supply of money produced, than there are goods and services currently available for purchase. In other words, the presence of more printed money at Washington money printing facilities exceeds the amount of goods you can ever buy in a country, or the productivity of an economy at the current time. In simple words, to reduce inflation, you must either reduce money printing, or you must increase productivity and innovation in a country by a lot. Under the free market system, less taxation on corporations fuels more growth of businesses, which increases jobs and makes an economy more powerful. By contrast, Keynesian economics suggests that more government intervention will stabilize the economy, which sometimes involves more regulations and taxations, but more government spending has clearly shown to be the cause of more inflation, and this inevitably causes recessions and more unemployment. And as the impressive growth and success of Hong Kong city suggests, the Friedmanite economics is clearly the winner.

During the 1990s, Hong Kong, along with other “special economic zones” in China, adopted a policy of hyper-capitalism, where corporations were completely free from any government interference, and were free to grow business by hiring people and driving more globalization. Many companies from USA and other countries migrated to this side of China and neighbouring areas due to more freedom and wealth promises under this free market system. Apple and other manufacturers started out-sourcing labor and other operations to Chinese factories, which drove further globalization and mass manufacturing. This helped China a lot, allowing it to grow exponentially more powerful within a matter of 20 years. Along with this, the free-trade system, where two or more countries trade imports and exports with each other under limited constraints and additional charges( tariffs), allowed many countries to grow more powerful. Friedman’s philoshopies supports this approach of a free-trade system, that can enabling more out-sourcing to China, more globalization, more supply-chain trade routes establishment between different countries. For example, many chip companies in thr USA such as Nvidia, Intel, etc, do the chip designing in-house, but out-source all manufacturing work to Taiwan, China, etc.

However, this had a disastrous effect for the USA economy. The way it happened is very insidious and genius. China manipulates its currency by using a clever trick: it pegs its Yuan currency such that it is not allowed to float more than 2% against a fixed level. Earlier it used to peg the Yuan against the dollar, but now it pegs it against a basket of other currencies. By contrast, the American dollar was earlier was tied up with gold and later on indirectly tied up with oil, as most of the major oil trading is done in USD dollars, but still the dollar operates under a floating exchange rate system, which means its value changes based on supply and demand in forex markets. This allows cheaper exports from China, which means much more flow of money into Chinese banks and government without any downsides. This makes Chinese exports more attractive to other countries. Indirectly, this causes “money drain” from the USA into China. This is why there must be, for a short period of time only, an addition of a “limited effect tariff system” on import and export of all goods to and from China and other countries, such as those in Europe. The tariff proprosals go against Friedman’s ideologies, but they are necessary because countries like China and Europian nations have indirectly taken advantage of trade with the USA, driving the economy to further ruin.

There must be, in my opinion, a delicate balance of free trade and merchantilism in the USA, preferably in a 40:60 ratio, where more merchantilism(meaning more nationalism when it comes to driving economy forward: like building more factories in-house and discouraging out-sourcing to other countries) should be there as compared to free trade. If free trade must be increased, tariffs should be increased moderately as well.

But enough about government and nations. What about capitalism on its own? Where does the thin line between capitalism and government actions end ? In what cases does multinational corporation (MNC) culture result into so much greed and monopolization that it goes against the spirit of real American capitalism ?

To understand this, let us take a detour. BlackRock is an American multinational company and an investment firm. It is the world’s largest asset manager, with more than 12 Trillion dollars in asset under management(AUM). That is more than the Gross Domestic Product( GDP) of all other countries in the world except China and the USA. Two other companies closely associated with Blackrock, Vanguard and State Street, when combined with BlackRock have an estimated 66 Trillion dollars in AUM! This company trio have rightfully earned the title of “ the third most powerful country in the world” ! It is literally an empire that operates from the shadows.

Let me repeat that: 3 companies, when put together, are known as an entity that is the third most powerful "Country” ! What gives them such vast power and influence ?

Search for any major company in the S&P 500, such as Google, Amazon, Microsoft, etc: and you will invariably see that the majority stakeholders in these businesses, with a percentage ownership of around 4-5% or even more, are BlackRock, Vanguard, and State Street. This much ownership stake implies majority voting rights given to these corporations. In other words, these 3 companies can easily influence the decisions of other companies. These 3 companies own shares of almost all companies, not only in the USA, but also in many other countries. I was personally surprised a lot when I saw that my savings account bank, Canara bank in India, had BlackRock as one of its institutional owners ! Further research led me to see that BlackRock has invested in many countries and corporations, including big infrastructure organiations like Jio Services in India. In other words, there is a high chance that any product or service you buy in today’s world, from any sector, like a car or a mobile phone or a t-shirt, has BlackRock as one of its major investors. BlackRock has an influence bar none, where it manages lot of assets, and if it was to crash unexpectedly, it will likely result in the whole world economy crashing down with it. BlackRock also engages in circular ownership with Vanguard and State Street, where BlackRock owns stocks of those other two, and in turn they own stocks in BlackRock and in each other. In other words, they own themselves, which has some legal implications as well. For all purposes, they can be considered as a single entity.

These companies are asset managers. They provide risk management services to other companies. They buy toxic assets, such as weak debts or bonds, and turn them into valuable assets. They invest heavily in big Exchange traded funds( ETFs) and other index funds. Essentially, they bet on the market, acting as a passive investor, but at a very tremendous scale. In many many cases, they own an organization or engage in a bank operation, such that they stand to gain more money and influence, and earn more profits, irrespective of whether a market or a company fails or succeeds. This ultra-passivity and dual-sided interests goes completely against the original true spirit of the American capitalism: that taking a high risk results in high rewards over time, but this is one-sided, meaning that if I was to start a new startup and own stake in it, I will obviously want it to succeed, and would stand to gain nothing if I fail. The way big asset managers like BlackRock work is unlike this philosophy, where in many instances they operate on both sides of the same deals.

This gives them an unprecedented monopoly and influence over many things. For example, if you invest in some fund, such as a 401(k) or a student loan or some college scheme, or any trust fund or retirement plans, or in other index funds, there is a very good possibility that some part of your money goes into the operations of BlackRock and its other assets. All this happens indirectly behind the scenes, you won’t even know it happened. BlackRock can easily influence operations of other companies: they started the ESG policy, where they gave high ratings to companies that followed their interests, and low ratings to companies that were anti-establishment(such as Tesla). High ratings implies further investments and protection offered by BlackRock. This ESG trend led to ruining of many brands such as BudLight, and losses of many other companies. BlackRock also funds a lot of government lobbying so that their execs can get into positions of power and influence, and shape government policies to suit their own interests. To show how this works, look at what they did during the 2008 financial crisis : following the market crash, the USA government called Larry Fink, the founder of BlackRock, to ask for advice on how to recover the country’s economy. BlackRock then helped the USA government by buying toxic assets from them and managing them under their portfolio, which indirectly saved the government from a lot of debt and ruin. Now in recent times, the Federal Reserve( which has no official power over the free markets and corporations when it comes to handling capital operations), employed BlackRock to purchase assets under a contract, which saved the Federal Reserve by a lot during the Covid pandemic. In other words, due to the absolute influence BlackRock has, it can sway political and government to further its own interests, gain more profits, control the mainstream news to theoretically brainwash the common public, and drive the world economy under their hands. We once again see here how government decisions can sometimes enable corporations like BlackRock to gain more influence over an economy. This is clearly the opposite of the American capitalism approach of more risk, more rewards, more freedom, more business growth in a competitive market of ever-changing supply and demand. BlackRock insulates itself from risk by working from both sides of the market. However, this must change: BlackRock must be broken down and its influence must be reduced because it goes against the premise of a capitalist philosophy. In some ways, while BlackRock emerged from capitalism, it shows us the dangers of capitalism taken at its limit, and steps that we must take to curb that influence and ensure that the American dream of capitalism must not be extinguished.

Another example of this, is the ulterior motives of NGOs and non-profits such as Bill Gates’ Foundation, that owns a lot of stake in the United Nations and other affiliated organizations, and are also tied up with such schemes that BlackRock enagages in. From the outside, people like Bill Gates will tell you thst they care about humanitarian efforts like reducing disease and poverty, but at the same time they take advantage of schemes that profit them a lot. Another example : Google restructured itself under a holding company named Alphabet, to split itself up so that it can remain a monopoly yet have different product lines. According to Tony Fadell, the founder of Nest Thermostat, and the person who designed the iphone under Steve Jobs, he sold his company to Google which acquired it and, quite literally, ruined it, all for profit and no innovation. Google’s work environment, corporate culture of management teams, and monopolistic mindset, is the complete opposite of a startup culture that drives more innovation, more valuable products and services, and more economy growth. In some ways, Apple has managed to stay out of this corporate mindset and remain a startup spirit. The creation of monopolies in markets, like BlackRock, and other large MNCs, stops new innovation, kills good ideas, and turns talented people into robotic workers, and causes corporate and political decisions that further ruin the economy. This, while still being a core part of a capitalist society, goes against the true spirit of capitalism.

In other words, this monopolization goes against the principles and ideologies of Milton Friedman, and other economists as well.

Greed is good. However, absolute power corrupts absolutely. There is a reason why, in an anime “fullmetal alchemist: Brotherhood”, there are 7 anthropomorphized incarnations of the seven deadly sins : pride, lust, greed, sloth, envy, gluttony, wrath ; and only one of them is inherently good: greed.

However, greed when used to gain monopolistic influence like BlackRock or Google does, is always bad as it inhibits further innovation and negatively affects the world economy or operations of some companies in the USA. This happens very slowly but surely under a capitalist environment, so we must be careful. There are methods to fight such power, but that’s a topic for another discussion later.

The very purpose of America, and capitalism, is to generate new idea factories, where people take huge risks and earn huge rewards by becoming entrepreneurs, by creating more jobs, and driving the economy of a country. There must a steady balance between startups turning into monopolies, a balance between free trade and tariffs, a balance between asset managment and government policies, a balance between capital gain profits and innovation. Because without any new invention or research, driven by reinvesting in itself by a company to accelerate value growth, there can be no more growth of capitalism as well.

posts.title: American Capitalism : the most powerful system
posts.summary: My beliefs regarding the USA, geopolitics and world economics.
posts.html:
“ Compound interest is the eight wonder of the world”

This quote is always attributed to Albert Einstein, and it stands true no matter which century or country we consider. The way it works to accelerate wealth and prosperity is so magical: after every time period, the current value of anything grows at a non-linear rate, “accelerating the process of acceleration”. Given sufficient time, a small corpus can grow into enormous magnitudes due to this effect.

Why am I talking about this though? It is because the power of compound interest is best seen in the context of a capitalist system, especially the American version of it. Underestimate the field of economics at your own peril. In my opinion, economics is something that everyone should know about. Put simply, capitalism is an economic system that relies on a dynamic and powerful system: “ the free market”. This is where private individuals and corporations own property and capitalize upon it. Capitalize refers to the ability to grow value of some asset during a certain time frame. This system relies upon the market, the buying and selling of goods and services. Supply and demand are the factors that determine the value of an asset, and the appropriate selling price of that asset.

In other words, capitalism is a system that encourages creation and growth of new startups and private corporations that work using the equity model. The whole concept of capitalism is dependent on the risk-reward philosophy, which means that a person invests into the future of a company( invests his money, or time, or mental prowess) in the hope that one day that company will grow into something bigger than his vision, into something that actually generates revenue and profit. You take high risk today individually without support from any social group, as you cannot determine the future of your endeavors, in the hopes that one day, that risk turns into high rewards for you. More risk, more reward. This system is the most powerful and proven model for our world, across all countries. Such a system works best without any government interference. Only in the USA , such a system works the best. America is a pioneer of the capitalist system. Their economy is the most powerful in the world: they have the reserve currency, the dollar is the most powerful currency in the world. Their Federal Reserve, arguably the world’s most powerful business, sets the standard for interest rates and inflation, thereby affecting the economies of all other countries like a ripple effect. The world trade itself gets affected by the operation and decisions of the Federal Reserve. Although it is heavily regulated, the Federal Reserve is a central bank and hence is effectively a business, and its operations determine the economy of the entire world.

Equity, which represents stock, determines the ownership percentage of a company. This percentage, the owner’s stake in some company, is translated into the number of shares he owns of that company. This number can be either dilutive or non-dilutive: which means that, companies have multiple rounds of valuations, where certain investors( venture capitalists or private individuals) estimate the probable “value” of a company and accordingly buy ownership in that company by investing and receiving stock, and this valuation of a company changes over time as the company grows more and more. Hence if a company’s overall value( the market capitalization) grows, consequently the ownership percentage will dilute, or reduce, as more shares are issued by the company to bring in more investors. In a special scenario, called the IPO, the company goes public, its board of directors changes, and it issues many more shares with the help of a bank institution for underwriting and stock exchange placing of the company. This is when anyone from the world can now invest into the company. Equity is the fastest and best way to create and sustain wealth, more than any other asset class such as real estate, commodities or treasury bills. Equity is the only effective way to build value and grow into greater prosperity. Without the concept of equity, no one can ever grow an idea or an innovation into a legacy. There are two ways to grow wealth in this way: to build a company yourself around some revolutionary idea, or buy your way into it as an investor. Effectively, entrepreneurs and investors are hence the fastest creators of wealth.

All this works around the concept of “perception” and “vision”. The United States of America represents that concept. “The American Dream” is a dream that anyone, no matter their country of origin, their status, their culture or religion, etc, can settle into America and have a vision to take risks and receive profits to achieve complete freedom : freedom to pursue their interests without any worry. The capitalist system works that exact way: selling people some “grand vision”. That vision, of a glorious future, translates into the risks one takes in the hopes of increasing value in the future. For example, an entrepreneur like Elon Musk will sell people a grand vision of humans landing on Mars or the best self-driving electric car in the world. That vision may or may not be achieved with a 100% guarantee, or may not ever be satisfactorily delivered, sometimes it will fail and people will snap back to cold harsh reality, yet they will still take risks because the system encourages “possibilities” and risks. The most important thing is that it always works. The market, a dynamic system of buyers and sellers across all countries in the world, always accurately estimates the “true value” of an idea, a vision, or a company. In other words, believing in a dream always works, versus living in a depressing reality.

You will always see entrepreneurs like Donald Trump or Steve Jobs sell their vision. They can warp their surrounding reality and people’s perceptions and make them believe in their vision. They are the epitome of an expert salesman. Better yet, they can execute upon their abstract ideas to build something tangible, something that causes a dent in an existing market, grab hold of the market share and achieve sustainable profits. Competition is for losers in this scenario, and only those who create a new innovation or invention, or an effective way to sell cheaper than their market competitors, can survive as a business. If you fall into the competition trap, what you sell becomes nothing more than a commodity, like mass-manufactured memory chips. It is hard to put a good price on something that gets cheapened by the market itself, essentially losing its value or unique selling point. Effectively, entrepreneurs build a brand around their identity, and the power of branding enables them to capture the public’s imagination and set a premium on what they sell, allowing them to build higher quality products with better profit margins.

The risk that such investors and businessmen take later translates into the disproportionately large rewards they receive after a lot of time. Entrepreneurs have to sacrifice their time, energy, comfort of a secure job position and a stable income source, their physical and mental health, and their vision, in order to build something new, gain market share, and sustain a growing company. Likewise, investors take the same risk by spending their money with the hope that the company will grow later on. The value of risk and time these people take, is much greater than anything that their peers do, hence they deserve the rewards they receive. You will see the issue of wealth redistribution discussed often all over the world. Many people believe that their is a huge wealth gap between lower and medium income working class families, and the ultra-rich elite class in the top 1% of richest people. They argue that such wealth must be given back to the community, and be spent in other social welfare programs. Essentially, they wish to increase taxes on rich people, or tax “unrealized capital gains”, or the monetary gains you receive by investing in equity. This system is bound to fail. The rich people should not be taxed such way, for such reasons, because as mentioned earlier, they are the ones who took huge risks and sacrified their lives to make something much bigger than themselves. In other words, the rich people deserve 100% of their hard-earned legal money and equity ownerships, as they were the ones who risked a lot to generate such a wealth gap. More risk, more rewards.

“The most noble thing you can do, is to create jobs.” This was said by Kevin O’Leary, best known for his role in Shark Tank. As an entrepreneur and investor, he believes that the job of an entrepreneur is to create new jobs and reduce unemployment in a country. The only way such businessmen can create new jobs is by taking advantage of the disproportionate equity returns of their business. Without such a capitalist system, everything falls apart. Entrepreneurs are who set the trend for the entire world, and hence deserve the highest form of respect and influence.

The administration running the USA government matters a lot, not just for the USA but also for all other countries. The USA is the most powerful country in the world for two reasons: the best military, and the most powerful currency. In a world where almost all countries are heavily influenced by religion and other differences, the USA is influenced by the economy more so than other reasons. Arguably, in my opinion, the economy is the most important part of what motivates the USA and guarantees its success, more so than religion or war. The USA conducts business with many countries: their foreign policy of trade with others determines their success. Trade involves many factors: import, export, manufacturing, tariffs, free trade,etc. For example, Apple, a company based in Cupertino, outsources the majority of its manufacturing to China: this is because it is relatively cheaper and easier to mass-manufacture computer components there, versus manufacturing in-house in the USA itself. Consequently, China has taken advantage of this in a most genius manner: they have manipulated their currency under their capitalist-one party State system in such a way that it benefits them a lot and negatively affects the USA by putting it in a budget deficit. Similarly, other chip manufacturers and designers like Nvidia or Intel, design in-house but outsource all the manufacturing to China and neighbouring countries. China has perhaps the most suprising growth in the entire world: they were relatively poor in the 1970s, but are now the second most powerful economy in the world currently. Even though it is a one-party state, it adopted the capitalist system, copying ideas from America, under only one city named Shenzhen in the beginning. In this “special economic zone”, China grew many successful and infleuential companies, turning huge profits. This also encouraged American businesses to migrate to that region due to cheaper and more accessible facilities. This quickly grew like a virus to the whole China, where they continued to copy the innovations of Americans and outgrew market competition by excessive globalization and cut-throat mass-manufacturing, enabled by heavy government subsidies. Consqequently, the Chinese currency has grown in value a lot.

As you can see here, the government of China plays a critical role in the success of their businesses. Here, government regulation and interference is too high, something that goes against the original American capitalism and the concept of free market. Such a system puts geopolitical pressure: Taiwan, where TSMC is located, manufactures the most crucial computers in the entire world, hence comes under a power play between China and the USA. This system must be discouraged, and more and more businesses must now slowly adopt the policy of manufacturing within the USA itself. This will reduce inflation, and allow more tax cuts for corporations so that they can create new jobs in the USA and reduce the deficit. The inflation in America directly affects all other countries and their economies, as the USA is the land of opportunities, where innovations happen, where science is best pursued, and because of which the dollar currency is the most important. This is why American politics matters, because it affects all other countries due to world economy shifts. Any large corporation turning over huge profit margins, must reinvest in themselves to further grow the business and compound upon itself, thereby creating more and more jobs for others. Hence entrepreneurs have the best job in the world, as they create jobs for many other people, and provide service to customers. Hence, they must not be taxed a lot, instead they must be encouraged to grow their business to essentially grow the entire world.

“Greed is good” - a quote by Gordon Gekko, a fictional character from Wall Street movie. In my opinion, naked greed is bad, because then you become nothing more than an immoral wall street trader hell-bent on making money, even by illegal means, expecting to receive more profits but doing no work himself, nothing more than manipulating the market to deceive innocent retail investors. In my opinion, greed+ a motivation to build something valuable to fulfill a vision, to create positive value for others, is a good thing. In fact, it the best thing ever, something that motivates capitalism. Encouraging tax cuts for such individuals and corporations ensures reduced national inflation, keeps the stock market healthy( not overinflated in value like a false bubble), and create many more opportunities.

In this aspect, I lean towards the policies set by the Republican Party under Trump in the USA, as of 2024. I may not agree with all their policies, but in the context of economy mandates, I whole-heartedly support their decisions surrounding the reduction of free trade system. “Free trade” is a set of mandates approved by countries such that they can trade goods and services with each other without any extra fees or tariffs. The problem with this is that, a smart country like China then easily takes advantage of loopholes so that their economy grows, whereas the USA falls into further debt. Make no mistake, China is the biggest customer of US businesses, yet they have carefully crafted their economy in such a way that they take advantage of market forces, and use them for their own benefits. Just take a look at how they have grown We-chat and Tencent. I say China, because they are the on the other side of the most important geopolitical trade war right now: the chip war. Computer chip manufacturing dominates everything in this world. The only manufacturers of chip making machines, the EUV Lithography machines, is ASML in Netherlands. Hence, the USA has put restrictions on this company to trade 3nm chip makers to Taiwan only( A US ally), and sell China those machines that make chips above 7nm.( worse performance than 3nm chips) .

In no other country you will ever see the country’s success and the thoughts and beliefs of its people being influenced by economics more than the USA. All other countries are fixated in other systems like socialism, communism, nationalist movements, etc, and are heavily limited by biases from religion or other fictional differences with no basis of science. Only in the USA, you will see a mixture of people of all races that achieve true freedom, by taking huge risks and achieving large rewards, by taking advantage of the system that enables compounding wealth: the American Capitalism.

posts.title: What Jim Simons' Medallion Fund may teach us about open-sourcing AI models?
posts.summary: A detailed look into how hype bubbles in finance and AI work, and why open-sourcing AI might be bad.
posts.html:
In the world of finance, there is a very famous theory known as the Efficient Market Hypothesis(EMH). Basically, what this hypothesis states is that for any security such as a company’s publicly traded stock, there is no way for anyone to accurately predict future prices based on any number of fundamental analysis or historical data you collect, simply because all the curent prices are accurately priced, by factoring in all factors including company’s performance and the public hype. In such an idealized world of a purely efficient market, be it for derivatives or the underlying assets, no one can possibly predict the future unless one engages in very risky strategies, hence EMH suggests that it is basically impossible to outperform the market, no matter what convoluted strategies you come up with.

A genius mathematician, Jim Simons, proved this hypothesis false. He founded Renaissance Technologies, and under this initiative started his own fund called Medallion Fund. What’s interesting about this fund is that it is completely closed to the public, only allowed to former or current employees of this company. In the history of humanity, this fund is the best to ever exist, returning an average annualized return of 66% ! This made Jim Simons the richest mathematician to ever live, with his net worth easily exceeding $30 billion!

What made him so special? He made use of highly complex mathematical equations,lots and lots of data(both historical and current, even of things like weather forecasts), a lot of computational power, hired some top scientists,physicists,statisticians, game theorists as his team, and also desgined ML algorithms to perform high-frequency trading of derivatives such as options, over short periods of time. All this is highly secretive and proprietary, and he has never revealed his strategies, only stating that he has made use of mathematical frameworks ( known as quant strategies in finance) like Markov chains and Markov decision processes, game theory, mean reversion, time series analysis and statistical arbitrage, and much more. No matter what strategy he used, it was a genius and highly profitable strategy.

But what makes it work so good? The very fact that it is closed-source and not released to the public, is the reason why it can consistently beat the market! In other words, if the secrets were revealed to the world, and was adopted by many mutual funds, hedge funds or even the individual investors, then the market would start converging towards a completely random, unpredictable behavior, thus making EMH true! Essentially, Medallion Fund proves EMH false, but according to a very famously observed behavior of the financial markets, if a certain well-proven and profitable strategy becomes popularly used, then that strategy starts failing and gives negative returns to new users, which means that if this fund’s strategy was revealed to everyone, it would stop working and render any previously useful variables for future predictions completely worthless.

This same principle applies to the world of tech and AI. Even though AI is a unique science, one that we are simultaneously studying and building at the same time, and even though AI is more about future overall scientific progress , than simple capitalism and profits, or even engineering, and even though open-sourcing new innovations in AI models is always a universally good thing, there comes a time when just open-sourcing all AI models, even if they are really good or powerful,makes very little sense. It would be much better if companies do NOT choose to open-source their proprietary work on AI, and choose to just keep their secrets to themselves. The world of AI is ever-changing, with extreme competition worlwide, sparked mostly by people who understand nothing about AI in the first place. This scenario is very similar to the world of finance, where it becomes really easy to create false hypes, bubbles and consequent losses. If there is one thing that Jim Simons’ strategy tells us, is that if someone comes up with a really innovative and groundbreaking AI model, they should not open-source it completely(only,say, 90% of the underlying theory that they used, and some progress steps, but not the entire model weights or other secrets), and it would be much better for the whole world if they choose to keep it hidden and earn profits from it( this also resonates with the entire idea of capitalism itself, where companies do not reveal their secrets to everyone, or else they get no competitive edge over others, and no way to earn profits overall). Consider what would happen if a country such as USA( via its top AI companies) develops a really powerful AI model(nuclear weapon level threat). Would it really be wise to open-source it? Wouldn’t that make it essentially worthless if literally every single person in this world comes to know about how it works? In such a scenario, no competition will thrive, which is similar to how EMH scenario would turn out to be, a completely random, hopeless market with no way to predict future prices at all!

There is a distinct similarity between the world of physics and the world of finance. An equation known as the Black-Scholes model accurately describes the behavior of derivatives market, and its foundations are derived from the same equation that can explain how heat transfer takes place, or even how blackjack can be played in casinos. This universality of such models makes them highly applicable to the world of finance as well, even though it is highly unpredictable, complex and dynamic. This makes finance one of the best domains where deep learning can be applied as well. A particular sub-field of ML is Physics-informed ML, where physics models can be used to make ML models much better at accurately modeling the real world. Similarly, a powerful quant sub-field can similarly evolve from taking in quant models to inform deep learning models, not just for short term derivatives, but long term value investing via fundamental analysis as well. When such models are created, it makes little sense to release them to the whole world at large, as then their distinct advantage will be rendered useless if everyone starts using them. Hence, they must always remain propreitary, and used solely by their creators only.

Open-sourcing every new powerful invention might not always be a good thing.

posts.title: The master algorithm
posts.summary: What could the road to AGI look like ?
posts.html:
In this article I write my thoughts on what the road to AGI could be, and what type of algorithm, architecture or substrate would lead to intelligence and consciousness.

Current AI development ( 99% of the best AI models and architectures used everywhere, with deep neural networks as the main ingredient) works the best because of a single, very powerful algorithm: backpropagation. Backpropagation is a very clever mechanism that enables the model to learn from the input data, especially so because of its use of chain rule, basic fundamental mathematical functions, and the power of derivatives. Hence the models using this method achieve greater performance and intelligence than humans across many fields(albeit narrow ones, and not generalized like humans). However, there is no indication whatsoever of the human brain using anything remotely resembling backpropagation to learn new things, exhibit intelligence and consciousness. Many experts in biology and neuroscience have examined this aspect, and conclude that there is no indication of backpropagation n human brains, but that the brain uses spiking neural networks, and learn and are intelligent by virtue of some unknown reason. In other words, no one yet knows what algorithm the brain uses.

Many people argue that the brain does not perform mechanical procedures or computations at all, like Roger Penrose argues in his famous book ” The Emperor’s New mind” ,where he essentially says that achieving AGI via computers( or any Turing machine) is theoretically impossible, and that some other unexplainable phenomenon operates inside brains. He says that as of now, science has not reached the stage where it can satisfactorily explain the level of intelligence and consciousness that human brains have. In other words, there is no existing scientific theory that can accurately model intelligence in its entire form, meaning that science has not progressed sufficiently yet. I believe that the last sentence is true, but my opinion is that it may soon change, and that within 20 or 30 years we will have a full comprehensive scientific theory that accurately explains AGI. I believe that intelligence and consciousness can be achieved by any complex system(irrespective of the underlying substrate, whether it be biological neurons , or electronic transistors) when it runs a really complex algorithm that inherently consists of self-references on a high level, a “master algorithm” that evolves over time, undergoes changes constantly to update itself, and is a self-referential system. In short, I am a firm believer of the strong-AI viewpoint.

What I also think is that the road to AGI may not be singular. I could be wrong, and the only way to know this is to wait a few more decades, but I believe that there could be different ways to reach AGI, that is, multiple “master algorithms”. As long as the algorithm is of an evolving nature, and exhibits self-references on a really high level of abstraction, that algorithm will show AGI-level capabilities irrespective of the underlying architecture or algorithm steps or training methods.

Let’s consider various famous models and architectures currently used in the AI world: ranging from simple deep neural networks with fully connected layers, convolutional neural networks, RNNs, LSTMs and GRUs, to transformers, diffusion models, autoencoders, GANs, and many more. Each one is suited to its use case, and one might be better than the other for a particular task( for example, transformers outperform RNNs for sequential data for natural language processing), and some of them are obviously more complex, intricate, bigger and just better. However, let us imagine that their computational powers were equally same( just a hypothetical scenario), and to make things even simpler, let’s assume all of them perform equally well on one particular use case. Then would it really matter which architecture, training method, or underlying algorithm was used to achieve that level of intelligence? Of course not. The type,shape and size of the training datasets might differ, but if hypothetically the end result is the same, does it matter which architecture was used?

In a similar fashion, I believe that the “master algorithm”, whatever it might be( a singular architecture, or a combination of various architectures clubbed together), I believe that it will not solely be the “only” algorithm that is the answer to AGI. In other words, there might be many different ways to achieve AGI, each one of them completely valid on its own. What is certain is that we must not underestimate deep learning, for it could lead us to achieve far greater things than what Roger Penrose thinks is possible, and one day computers might surpass human brains in every way possible.

There is an inherent difference between consciousness and intelligence. A living creature may be conscious but not intelligent, and a software algorithm may be intelligent but not conscious. Solving the mystery of consciousness, and how it is created and maintained in a brain, is the greatest unknown mystery in this universe, far beyond knowing about how the universe itself began or what happens if you fall inside a black hole. But, for a human-degree of consciousness, intelligence might be needed to support being conscious as well. Who knows? Is consciousness even a necessary component to acheiving Superintelligence? One thing for sure is that a “master algorithm” must definitely be a conscious entity, otherwise it does not qualify to be a master algorithm. How would we even design an algorithm to emulate consciousness? In a previous article I wrote on Roger Penrose, he says that a collapse of wave function is needed for consciousness to emerge, brought in our brains by quantum-mechanical effects. On the other hand , Hofstadter claims the self-reference in a system is needed for such emergence. Whatever may be the case, I still believe that creating such an algorithm is within reach, and right now deep learning is the best approach to it.

In his book “The master algorithm”,Pedro Domingos says that there are 5 main approaches to achieving this:

  1. Symbolists ( Logic, axioms, rules, discrete math)

  2. Connectionists( deep learning)

  3. Evolutionaries( genetic algorithms)

  4. Bayesians( Probablistic models)

  5. Analogizers ( SVMs)

Of all these, he takes an approach to combine them all together and proposes a new model : Markov Logic Networks (MLN). Together with a given domain, a Markov logic network defines a probability distribution on the set of all interpretations of its predicates on the given domain. The underlying idea is that an interpretation is more likely if it satisfies formulas with positive weights and less likely if it satisfies formulas with negative weights. In other words, put simply, it combines probabilistic models like Markov models with flexible logic rules.
